meta.blurb: Elinor Dashwood hides every feeling, and her sister Marianne hides none. After their father dies, the two leave their home with almost no money. Then each falls in love, and each man has a secret.
meta.bible: Elinor Dashwood: nineteen at the start; sensible, calm and loyal; hides her feelings to protect others; loves Edward Ferrars. Marianne Dashwood: sixteen at the start; passionate, romantic and honest about every feeling; falls in love with Willoughby. Margaret Dashwood: the youngest sister, thirteen, cheerful and imaginative. Mrs Dashwood: their warm, romantic mother, who is as quick to feel as Marianne. Mr Henry Dashwood: their father, who dies in the first beat and leaves them little. John Dashwood: Mr Henry Dashwood's son by his first wife; the half brother of the sisters; weak and easily led. Fanny Dashwood: John's wife, selfish and proud, who persuades him to give nothing; sister of Edward and Robert Ferrars. Edward Ferrars: Fanny's brother; shy, kind and honest; secretly engaged to Lucy Steele. Robert Ferrars: Edward's younger brother, vain and silly. Mrs Ferrars: their rich, domineering mother. Sir John Middleton: a cheerful, generous cousin who owns Barton Park and lets the Dashwoods a cottage. Lady Middleton: his cold, polite wife. Mrs Jennings: her loud, warm and meddling mother, who loves matchmaking. Colonel Brandon: about thirty-five, a quiet, loyal soldier who loves Marianne; he owns Delaford. John Willoughby: a handsome, charming young man who woos Marianne and then drops her for a rich bride, Miss Grey. Mrs Smith: Willoughby's rich old aunt, who lives at Allenham. Eliza Williams: a girl whom Willoughby ruined and abandoned; Colonel Brandon's ward and the daughter of his first love. Lucy Steele and Anne Steele: sisters, cousins of Mrs Jennings; Lucy is sly and clever and is secretly engaged to Edward. Mr and Mrs Palmer: Mrs Jennings's other daughter, Charlotte, and her husband, who own Cleveland. Places: Norland Park in Sussex, the Dashwoods' old home; Barton Cottage and Barton Park in Devonshire; Allenham; Whitwell; Exeter; London; Cleveland in Somerset; Delaford, the Colonel's parsonage and estate. Voice and tone: warm, ironic and clear; the sisters are different but both are right in some things and wrong in others; the book ends happily and fairly. Added facts: Harry Dashwood: John and Fanny's little son, four years old, who is to inherit Norland after his father under the old uncle's will. Mr Pratt: Edward's tutor near Plymouth, uncle of Lucy and Anne Steele. Longstaple: the place near Plymouth where Edward lived with Mr Pratt. Thomas: the Dashwoods' manservant. Miss Grey: a rich young woman with fifty thousand pounds, whom Willoughby marries. Miss Morton: the daughter of Lord Morton with thirty thousand pounds, whom Mrs Ferrars wants Edward to marry. Charlotte Palmer: Mrs Jennings's daughter, who laughs at everything. Mr Harris: the apothecary at Cleveland. Combe Magna: Willoughby's own small estate in Somerset. Berkeley Street: where Mrs Jennings lives in London. Harley Street: where John and Fanny stay in London. Conduit Street: where Lady Middleton lives in London. Gray's: a jeweller's shop in London. Bond Street; Oxford; Plymouth. Delaford: Colonel Brandon's estate, with a parsonage worth two hundred pounds a year. Willoughby is about twenty-five; Elinor is nineteen and Marianne sixteen at the start, and Marianne is nineteen when she marries. The family have five hundred pounds a year and ten thousand pounds in all. The Dashwoods are cousins of Sir John Middleton through Mrs Dashwood.
chapters: A Cold Look Across the Room

beats.scene: Old Norland Park in autumn, golden woods around a grey stone house
beats.summary: The Dashwoods have owned Norland Park in Sussex for generations, and its old bachelor owner lives there happily with his nephew Henry's family.

beats.scene: A grave lawyer reads a will aloud to the silent Dashwood family
beats.summary: When the old man dies, his will leaves Norland to Henry only for his lifetime and then to little Harry, his grandnephew, with just a thousand pounds for each of Henry's three daughters.

beats.scene: Mr Henry Dashwood lies weak in bed while his son stands beside him
beats.summary: A year later Henry Dashwood falls ill, and on his deathbed he asks his son John to look after his second wife and their three daughters.

beats.scene: John Dashwood walks alone in the Norland garden, deep in thought
beats.summary: John promises his father to help them, and after the funeral he decides to give his three half sisters a thousand pounds each.

beats.scene: Fanny Dashwood sits upright by the fire, shaking her head at her husband
beats.summary: John's wife Fanny is horrified, for she believes that so much money would be taken from their little boy Harry.

beats.scene: John counts coins at a desk while Fanny argues beside him
beats.summary: Step by step Fanny talks him down from three thousand pounds to fifteen hundred, then to a small yearly sum, and then to a hundred pounds a year.

beats.scene: John and Fanny nod together over a letter as the fire burns low
beats.summary: In the end Fanny persuades him that the women will be comfortable on five hundred a year, so he will give nothing but a little help and gifts of fish and game.

beats.scene: A carriage with trunks and a small boy arrives at Norland's door
beats.summary: Fanny arrives at Norland with her child and servants before the widow has even left, and she takes charge of the house like its mistress.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood sits alone with tears in her eyes, Elinor beside her
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood is so hurt by Fanny's rudeness that she wants to leave that day, but Elinor persuades her to wait and think.

beats.scene: Elinor reads quietly while Marianne plays the piano, in one room
beats.summary: The sisters are very different: Elinor is calm and sensible, Marianne is passionate and open, and little Margaret is cheerful and fond of games.

beats.scene: Edward Ferrars steps down from his horse at Norland's front gate
beats.summary: Fanny's brother Edward Ferrars comes to stay at Norland, and Mrs Dashwood sees at once how gentle and modest he is.

beats.scene: Edward and Elinor walk slowly along a garden path, talking quietly
beats.summary: Edward and Elinor spend many hours together, and she comes to love his honest heart, though he is neither handsome nor bold.

beats.scene: Edward reads aloud by the fire while Marianne frowns across the room
beats.summary: Marianne thinks Edward cold because he reads poetry without feeling, but Elinor says that good sense and kindness matter more.

beats.scene: Two chairs by a window, Edward speaking low and Elinor listening
beats.summary: Edward tells Elinor that he longs for a quiet life as a clergyman, though his proud mother wants him to be a famous man.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood smiles at Edward and Elinor across the tea table
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood hopes they will marry, but Elinor warns that she cannot be sure of Edward's feelings or of his mother's consent.

beats.scene: Fanny whispers sharply to Mrs Dashwood in the Norland hall
beats.summary: Fanny lets Mrs Dashwood know that her mother expects Edward to marry a rich lady, and Mrs Dashwood, insulted, decides to leave.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood reads a letter by candlelight and looks up in surprise
beats.summary: A letter comes from her cousin Sir John Middleton in Devonshire, offering a small cottage at Barton for a low rent.

beats.scene: Elinor watches her mother write a quick reply at the writing desk
beats.summary: Elinor thinks Devonshire is far from Edward, but her mother is impatient to go and accepts the cottage by return of post.

beats.scene: Servants pack books, china and a piano into boxes in the hall
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood sells her carriage and packs her china, linen, books and Marianne's piano, while John says that he wishes he could do more.

beats.scene: Marianne weeps under the old trees as Norland fades behind her
beats.summary: Edward is invited to visit Barton, and before the family leaves, Marianne says a tearful goodbye to the trees and house she loves.

beats.scene: A loaded carriage travels along a green country road at dusk
beats.summary: The family travel for several days to Devonshire, and Marianne is sad while her mother hopes and Margaret asks a hundred questions.

beats.scene: A small plain cottage with a tiled roof stands in a green valley
beats.summary: Barton Cottage is small and plain, with four bedrooms and two attics, but its valley is lovely and the hills around it are high.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood and the servants carry boxes into a low, narrow hall
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood is delighted with the cottage and dreams of adding rooms, though the house is low and crooked and there are only three servants.

beats.scene: Sir John Middleton stands at the cottage door, laughing, with a basket
beats.summary: Sir John Middleton, their cousin and landlord, calls the next day with fruit and game and invites them to dinner at Barton Park.

beats.scene: Sir John laughs at the head of a table beside Mrs Jennings
beats.summary: At Barton Park Sir John welcomes them warmly, and they meet his cold, polite wife and her loud, merry mother Mrs Jennings.

beats.scene: Lady Middleton's noisy children tug at her chair while she smiles
beats.summary: Lady Middleton speaks only of her spoiled and noisy children, and Elinor finds the family kind but not at all interesting.

beats.scene: A quiet tall officer listens to Marianne play the piano at Barton Park
beats.summary: They meet Colonel Brandon, a quiet man of thirty-five, who alone listens to Marianne's music with real feeling.

beats.scene: Marianne and Elinor laugh together by the cottage fire
beats.summary: Marianne declares the Colonel far too old to feel love, because he is thirty-five and mentions a pain in his shoulder, but Elinor defends him.

beats.scene: Mrs Jennings laughs as she whispers a joke to Elinor, nodding toward the Colonel
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings, who loves matchmaking, teases Marianne about the Colonel, and the sisters bear it with patience.

beats.scene: Marianne stands on a high green hill with her hair blowing
beats.summary: The family settle to a quiet life, and Marianne finds that she loves the wild hills above the cottage.

beats.scene: Marianne and Margaret climb a green hill under heavy grey clouds
beats.summary: One windy morning Marianne and Margaret climb the high hill, though the clouds look dark and Elinor stays at home.

beats.scene: Marianne lies on a wet hillside as a young man runs toward her
beats.summary: Running down the hill in the rain, Marianne falls and twists her ankle, while a man with a gun and two dogs hurries to help.

beats.scene: A tall young man carries Marianne through the cottage garden
beats.summary: The stranger lifts her, carries her down to the cottage and straight into the sitting room, to the surprise of her mother and sister.

beats.scene: The young man bows low in the small sitting room, giving his name
beats.summary: He says that his name is Willoughby, that he is staying at Allenham, and he asks leave to call tomorrow to ask after her ankle.

beats.scene: Sir John Middleton laughs in his parlour, telling stories about a young man
beats.summary: Sir John says that Willoughby is a lively sportsman who will inherit Allenham, and Mrs Jennings jokes that Marianne has set her cap at him.

beats.scene: Willoughby sits close to Marianne, laughing over a book of poems
beats.summary: Willoughby visits the next day, and he and Marianne discover that they love the same poets, the same music and the same dances.

beats.scene: Elinor sits in a corner with her sewing, watching them quietly
beats.summary: Elinor is glad that Marianne is so happy, but she thinks the two of them speak far too openly about everything.

beats.scene: Willoughby and Marianne dance together all evening at Barton Park
beats.summary: At a small dance at Barton Park, Willoughby dances almost only with Marianne, and Lady Middleton is quietly displeased.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon sits sadly in a corner while Willoughby and Marianne laugh
beats.summary: Willoughby and Marianne joke about Colonel Brandon as dull, and Elinor defends him as a man of knowledge, goodness and sense.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon speaks gravely to Elinor by a window while Marianne talks
beats.summary: Marianne says that nobody can love twice, and the Colonel, saddened, tells Elinor that such a belief will not last.

beats.scene: Willoughby cuts a lock of Marianne's hair with a pair of small scissors
beats.summary: Willoughby asks for a lock of Marianne's hair, and she gives it freely, as if there were nothing to hide.

beats.scene: Elinor and Mrs Dashwood talk in low voices by the fire at Barton Cottage
beats.summary: Margaret tells Elinor what she has seen, and Elinor worries that there is no promise, but her mother trusts them.

beats.scene: Willoughby holds a fine brown horse while Marianne looks at it eagerly
beats.summary: Willoughby offers Marianne a horse, but Elinor reminds her that they cannot afford a groom, so Marianne gives up the gift.

beats.scene: Willoughby stands with his hand on the cottage wall, the family listening
beats.summary: When Mrs Dashwood speaks of building new rooms, Willoughby begs her to change nothing, because he loves the little house exactly as it is.

beats.scene: Guests wait at breakfast as a servant hands the Colonel a letter
beats.summary: Sir John plans a picnic at Whitwell, but the Colonel reads a letter at breakfast, turns pale and leaves at once for London.

beats.scene: Mrs Jennings whispers to Sir John, counting her guesses on her fingers
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings guesses that the letter concerns a Miss Williams, a young person the Colonel is known to care for, and the picnic is cancelled.

beats.scene: Willoughby drives a light open carriage with Marianne beside him
beats.summary: Instead Sir John proposes a drive, and Willoughby takes Marianne in his open carriage while the others go home.

beats.scene: Marianne and Willoughby walk hand in hand through a large empty house
beats.summary: Marianne and Willoughby tour the rooms of Allenham while Mrs Smith is out, and Elinor says that this was improper.

beats.scene: Elinor speaks gently to Marianne in the cottage bedroom
beats.summary: Marianne laughs off Elinor's warning, saying that true feeling is never wrong, and Elinor decides to be quiet.

beats.scene: Willoughby reads aloud to the family by the light of a candle
beats.summary: In the evenings Willoughby reads aloud, Marianne listens in delight, and Mrs Dashwood is sure that they will soon be married.

beats.scene: Willoughby arrives at the cottage looking pale, with a letter in hand
beats.summary: One morning Willoughby arrives in distress: Mrs Smith has sent him to London on business, and he must leave at once.

beats.scene: Willoughby leaves the cottage in distress while Marianne stands weeping in the doorway
beats.summary: He cannot say when he will return, refuses Mrs Dashwood's invitation to stay and rides away, and Marianne sobs.

beats.scene: Elinor and Mrs Dashwood talk anxiously in the quiet sitting room
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood thinks that Mrs Smith wants to part the lovers, but Elinor is not sure and keeps her doubts to herself.

beats.scene: Marianne walks alone on the hills, refusing food and speaking to no one
beats.summary: Marianne gives herself up to grief: she plays sad songs, walks alone and thinks only of Willoughby.

beats.scene: Edward Ferrars sits quietly with Elinor in the cottage sitting room
beats.summary: After a week Edward arrives without warning, and Elinor's heart lifts, but Edward is quiet and low in spirits.

beats.scene: Edward turns a ring in his hand while Marianne watches him
beats.summary: Marianne notices a ring with a lock of hair, and Edward says it is his sister's, but Elinor hopes that it is her own.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood speaks to Edward in the garden, urging him to stay
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood says that Edward should be his own master, but he answers that he cannot go against his mother's wishes.

beats.scene: Edward rides away from Barton Cottage while Elinor watches from the garden gate
beats.summary: Edward leaves after a week, and Elinor, hiding her disappointment, busies herself so that her mother will not see.

beats.scene: Elinor draws at the table while Marianne stares out of the window
beats.summary: While Marianne mourns openly, Elinor tells herself that Edward's heart is true, but she must not hope too much.

beats.scene: Mrs Jennings and Sir John tease Elinor while Margaret giggles at the table
beats.summary: At Barton Park they tease Elinor about her sweetheart, and Margaret blurts out that his name is Ferrars.

beats.scene: Mrs Palmer laughs at everything while her husband reads a newspaper
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings's daughter, Mrs Palmer, visits Barton Park and laughs at everything, while her husband is rude and sleepy.

beats.scene: Mrs Palmer begs the sisters to visit Cleveland, clapping her hands
beats.summary: Mrs Palmer invites the sisters to her home at Cleveland, and she says kindly that she knows all about Mr Willoughby.

beats.scene: Two sisters in bright ribbons curtsy in the drawing room of Barton Park
beats.summary: Lucy Steele and her sister Anne, poor cousins of Mrs Jennings, arrive at Barton Park for a long visit.

beats.scene: Lucy flatters Lady Middleton's children while Anne chatters beside her
beats.summary: Lucy wins Lady Middleton with her care for the children, and she seems especially keen to make a friend of Elinor.

beats.scene: Anne Steele teases Elinor, nodding, while Lucy watches her face
beats.summary: Anne teases Elinor about her sweetheart Mr Ferrars, and Lucy asks about Fanny and Mrs Ferrars with sharp interest.

beats.scene: Lucy whispers to Elinor behind a card table, holding a small miniature
beats.summary: Lucy tells Elinor in secret that she has been engaged to Edward Ferrars for four years.

beats.scene: Lucy shows Elinor a letter in Edward's handwriting and a small ring
beats.summary: Lucy proves her story with Edward's letters and portrait, and Elinor realises that the ring Edward wears holds Lucy's hair.

beats.scene: Elinor stands calm and pale, listening, her hands folded
beats.summary: Elinor keeps her face still and promises to keep the secret, though her heart is breaking.

beats.scene: Elinor sits alone at her desk at night, writing and thinking
beats.summary: Elinor understands Edward's low spirits at last, and she grieves silently, while pitying him for being trapped.

beats.scene: Lucy and Elinor walk in the gardens of Barton Park, speaking low
beats.summary: Lucy comes back to the secret, hoping for Elinor's pity, and Elinor tells her coldly that she will never speak of it.

beats.scene: Mrs Jennings invites the sisters to London, holding a bag of travelling things
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings invites Elinor and Marianne to stay with her in London, and Marianne agrees at once, hoping to see Willoughby.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood hugs her daughters at the cottage door, smiling bravely
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood presses both daughters to go, and Elinor, after some doubt, agrees to accompany Marianne.

beats.scene: Two sisters sit in Mrs Jennings's carriage, rolling toward London
beats.summary: The sisters travel in Mrs Jennings's carriage and reach London after three days, with Marianne silent and thinking of Willoughby.

beats.scene: Elinor and Marianne in a tall London drawing room, hearing street noise
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings's house in Berkeley Street is large and busy, and Marianne starts at every knock on the door.

beats.scene: Marianne writes a letter at a desk while Elinor watches with worry
beats.summary: Marianne writes to Willoughby at once, and then again and again, but no answer comes.

beats.scene: Elinor and Marianne talk seriously on a sofa by the window
beats.summary: Elinor asks Marianne whether she is engaged to Willoughby, and Marianne answers that she is sure of his love, so no promise is needed.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon sits close to Elinor in a quiet room, speaking gravely
beats.summary: Colonel Brandon visits and asks Elinor, with great concern, whether Marianne and Willoughby are engaged.

beats.scene: A visiting card lies on a table in Mrs Jennings's hall
beats.summary: When they come home, they find Willoughby's card, and Marianne is overjoyed, but he does not call again.

beats.scene: Mrs Palmer sits laughing in Mrs Jennings's drawing room as her husband yawns
beats.summary: The Palmers visit in London, and Mrs Palmer's cheerfulness cannot lift Marianne, who waits every day by the window.

beats.scene: Marianne dresses for an evening party with trembling hands
beats.summary: A party at Lady Middleton's is planned, and Marianne hopes that Willoughby will be there.

beats.scene: Marianne searches a crowded ballroom with her eyes, standing very still
beats.summary: At the party Marianne searches every face for Willoughby, and Elinor tries to calm her.

beats.scene: Marianne stares across a crowded ballroom at Willoughby and a fashionable lady
beats.summary: Willoughby is there with a fashionable young woman, and he looks across the room and quickly turns his face away.

beats.scene: Marianne holds out her hand as Willoughby bows stiffly before her
beats.summary: Marianne cries out his name and offers her hand, but Willoughby asks only coldly after her mother and bows.

beats.scene: Elinor helps Marianne to a chair as the room turns to look
beats.summary: Marianne almost faints, and Elinor leads her out of the room while strangers whisper.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon holds a door open for the sisters in the dim hall
beats.summary: The Colonel sees Marianne's pain, fetches the carriage quietly and says nothing to anyone.

beats.scene: Marianne sits writing at a desk with tears falling on the paper
beats.summary: That night Marianne writes again, begging Willoughby to explain, and she waits all morning for his answer.

beats.scene: A footman brings a letter on a silver tray to Marianne
beats.summary: At last a letter arrives, and Marianne tears it open with trembling hands.

beats.scene: Marianne cries on a sofa with a letter and a lock of hair
beats.summary: Willoughby coldly returns her letters and her lock of hair and says that he is engaged to another woman.

beats.scene: Mrs Jennings pats Marianne's hand and gives her a glass of wine
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings comforts Marianne with kindness and sweets, though her loud sympathy only adds to Marianne's pain.

beats.scene: Mrs Jennings counts on her fingers, shaking her head in anger
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings tells Elinor that Willoughby is to marry a Miss Grey, who has fifty thousand pounds.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon waits in a London parlour, his hat in his hands
beats.summary: The next morning Colonel Brandon calls and asks to speak alone with Elinor about a matter that might help her sister.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon sits straight and speaks quietly to Elinor
beats.summary: The Colonel says that Marianne reminds him of a girl he once loved, Eliza, who grew up as his father's ward.

beats.scene: A young girl weeps beside an older man in a drawing room
beats.summary: Eliza was forced to marry the Colonel's older brother, and the Colonel, heartbroken, was sent abroad to serve.

beats.scene: A thin woman lies in a poor room, holding a small child's hand
beats.summary: Eliza's marriage failed, and when the Colonel found her again she was poor and dying, and she asked him to look after her little daughter.

beats.scene: A schoolgirl stands in a sunlit garden, smiling over her shoulder
beats.summary: He placed the child, also named Eliza, in a good home, and as she grew up she became a pretty, trusting girl.

beats.scene: An empty room where a young girl's bed has not been slept in
beats.summary: At sixteen the girl disappeared, and months later the Colonel found her, with a baby, alone and in disgrace.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon looks sternly at Elinor as he speaks the name
beats.summary: The man who had ruined her was Willoughby, and the Colonel fought a duel with him, but no one was hurt.

beats.scene: Elinor and Colonel Brandon sit together in a quiet room, the letter between them
beats.summary: The letter at Whitwell was news of poor Eliza, and the Colonel asks Elinor to tell Marianne the truth, so that she will heal.

beats.scene: Elinor sits by Marianne's bed and speaks softly to her sister
beats.summary: Elinor tells Marianne the whole story, and Marianne listens with wide eyes and begins to see Willoughby as he really was.

beats.scene: Marianne sits with a cup of tea, her face pale but calm
beats.summary: Marianne eats a little, thanks the Colonel for his kindness and says she will try to be calm for her mother's sake.

beats.scene: John Dashwood sits stiffly in Mrs Jennings's London parlour, hat on his knee
beats.summary: John Dashwood visits the sisters in London, and he is polite and warm, because he now believes that Mrs Jennings is rich.

beats.scene: John Dashwood leans toward Elinor, speaking in a low and eager voice
beats.summary: John says what a fine thing it would be if Marianne married Colonel Brandon, who has two thousand pounds a year.

beats.scene: John and Elinor walk together along a busy London street
beats.summary: John takes Elinor shopping to a famous jeweller's shop in London, because Fanny has asked him to buy something.

beats.scene: A young man in fine clothes studies toothpick cases in a shop
beats.summary: At Gray's Elinor and her brother find a vain young man spending a very long time choosing a toothpick case.

beats.scene: The fashionable young man holds up a tiny gold case to the light
beats.summary: He is Robert Ferrars, Edward's younger brother, and he takes a quarter of an hour to choose his toothpick case.

beats.scene: Robert Ferrars bows lazily to Elinor, smiling at himself in a mirror
beats.summary: Robert barely looks at Elinor, and later he talks with a laugh about people who live in tiny cottages.

beats.scene: Lucy and Anne Steele arrive at Harley Street with their trunks
beats.summary: Fanny, who knows nothing of Lucy's secret, invites the Steele sisters to stay with her in Harley Street.

beats.scene: Fanny and Lady Middleton sit stiffly together, sipping tea
beats.summary: Fanny and Lady Middleton become good friends, since both of them are cold, polite and proud.

beats.scene: A formal card on a silver tray reads an invitation to dinner
beats.summary: Fanny invites Elinor and Marianne to dinner in Harley Street, and Elinor knows that Mrs Ferrars will be there.

beats.scene: Elinor sits at the window in Berkeley Street, worrying about the dinner
beats.summary: Elinor dreads meeting Edward's mother, and she wonders what the dinner will do to her.

beats.scene: A formal dining table with candles in Fanny's Harley Street house
beats.summary: At the dinner Elinor meets Mrs Ferrars, a thin, proud woman who looks at her coldly.

beats.scene: Mrs Ferrars looks down her nose at a screen painted by Elinor
beats.summary: Fanny shows off Elinor's painted screens, and Mrs Ferrars says that Miss Morton paints far better.

beats.scene: Mrs Ferrars smiles warmly at Lucy Steele across the table
beats.summary: Mrs Ferrars is kind to Lucy, who flatters her cleverly, and Elinor realises the cruel joke of the situation.

beats.scene: Lucy shows Elinor a bracelet and smiles with secret triumph
beats.summary: Lucy whispers that Mrs Ferrars has been so kind, as if she herself were already a daughter of the family.

beats.scene: Marianne sits silent and pale in a corner of Fanny's drawing room
beats.summary: Marianne is unhappy and rude at the dinner, and Elinor hides her own sadness to protect them both.

beats.scene: Edward steps into Mrs Jennings's London parlour and stops, looking startled
beats.summary: Some days later Edward calls at Mrs Jennings's house and finds Elinor and Marianne there with Lucy.

beats.scene: Four people sit in awkward silence in a small London drawing room
beats.summary: The meeting is very painful: Edward blushes, Lucy watches him, and Elinor bravely greets him as a friend.

beats.scene: Marianne speaks warmly to Edward and notices his unhappy face
beats.summary: Marianne greets Edward very kindly and wonders why he seems so low, although she does not know the cause.

beats.scene: Edward rises quickly and bows, leaving the room in a hurry
beats.summary: Edward leaves after a few minutes, and Elinor, though she is sorry for him, admires the way he behaved.

beats.scene: Elinor stands at a window and watches him walk down the street
beats.summary: Elinor tells herself that he is bound to Lucy by honour, and she must keep her silence.

beats.scene: Anne Steele whispers in Fanny's drawing room, hands clasped to her mouth
beats.summary: Anne Steele, believing that Fanny already knows, blurts out the secret engagement to her.

beats.scene: Fanny screams and falls into a chair, her servants rushing around her
beats.summary: Fanny falls into hysterics, and her husband John is horrified by the news.

beats.scene: John Dashwood hurries into Mrs Jennings's parlour with an anxious face
beats.summary: John rushes to Berkeley Street to tell Elinor the terrible news, and he is sure that she will share his outrage.

beats.scene: Mrs Ferrars sweeps into Fanny's drawing room in a rage
beats.summary: Mrs Ferrars arrives at Harley Street in a fury and has the two Steele sisters driven from the house.

beats.scene: Mrs Jennings throws up her hands in a kind of delighted horror
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings hears the whole story with excitement and declares that Edward and Lucy deserve better treatment.

beats.scene: Edward stands firm before his mother in a grand drawing room
beats.summary: Edward refuses to break his promise to Lucy, and Mrs Ferrars cuts him off and gives his inheritance to his brother Robert.

beats.scene: Elinor sits silently with a cup of tea going cold in her hand
beats.summary: Elinor listens to every detail, and Mrs Jennings does not guess how deeply Elinor feels it.

beats.scene: Marianne stares at Elinor in astonishment as the truth comes out
beats.summary: Marianne hears that Elinor has known of the engagement for four months, and she is amazed that Elinor kept silent.

beats.scene: Marianne weeps with her arms round Elinor on the sofa
beats.summary: Marianne is ashamed of her own selfishness, and she says that she could never have borne such pain so quietly.

beats.scene: The sisters sit side by side in a dim room, holding hands
beats.summary: Elinor says that she did not give way because it would have hurt others, and the two sisters are closer than before.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon speaks to Elinor in a small room, holding a paper
beats.summary: Colonel Brandon hears of Edward's trouble and asks Elinor to offer him the living at Delaford, worth about two hundred pounds a year.

beats.scene: Elinor takes the paper from the Colonel's hands with a trembling smile
beats.summary: Elinor is moved by his kindness, and she thanks him, though she would rather the offer came from someone else.

beats.scene: Edward stands in Mrs Jennings's parlour, staring at the paper
beats.summary: Elinor tells Edward of the Colonel's offer, and Edward, humbled, accepts it with deep gratitude.

beats.scene: Edward speaks to Elinor with great feeling, his voice shaking
beats.summary: Edward says that he could marry Lucy on a small income, and he thanks Elinor for her kindness.

beats.scene: John Dashwood strides into a London parlour, wearing a pleased smile

beats.scene: Elinor speaks gently to Marianne on a window seat, holding her hand

beats.scene: Elinor writes a letter to her mother at the desk

beats.scene: Mrs Jennings packs a trunk and chatters, with the Palmers' letter on the table

beats.scene: Marianne stands at a window, looking at a grey hill far off

beats.scene: Elinor lays a hand on Marianne's forehead and looks worried

beats.scene: Mrs Palmer hurries away with her baby, a trunk and her husband

beats.scene: Elinor sits by the bed holding Marianne's hand through a long dark night
beats.summary: Elinor nurses Marianne tirelessly, and Mrs Jennings, though loud, shows herself a faithful and generous friend.

beats.scene: Elinor watches a bright morning sun rise in the window
beats.summary: Marianne grows worse, and Elinor, who has never been so afraid, begins to think of writing to their mother.

beats.scene: Elinor writes a hurried note at the bedside table by candlelight
beats.summary: At last Elinor decides that she must send for Mrs Dashwood, and she is writing the note when she hears a carriage at the door.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon arrives at Cleveland in the evening, his coat wet
beats.summary: It is Colonel Brandon, who has come to see how Marianne is, and he is shocked to hear how ill she is.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon bows to Elinor in the hall, speaking urgently
beats.summary: The Colonel offers to fetch Mrs Dashwood himself in his own carriage, and Elinor, who has not yet sent her note, thanks him with tears.

beats.scene: A carriage drives off in the dark with its lamps burning
beats.summary: He leaves at midnight, and Elinor goes back to the sickroom, feeling thankful but very afraid.

beats.scene: Marianne tosses on the bed, calling for her mother in her sleep
beats.summary: Marianne raves in her fever, calling for her mother, and Elinor holds her hand and speaks softly to her.

beats.scene: Elinor and Mrs Jennings sit up together by a single candle
beats.summary: Mrs Jennings and Elinor keep watch together, and Elinor learns how warm a heart lies under the old woman's chatter.

beats.scene: Mr Harris examines Marianne by lamplight while Elinor holds her breath
beats.summary: Mr Harris comes again and says that he sees no change, and Elinor's hope fades.

beats.scene: Elinor walks anxiously up and down the dark hall, listening
beats.summary: Elinor prays quietly for her sister and thinks over all the things they have shared since they were small.

beats.scene: A beam of morning light falls across Marianne's sleeping face
beats.summary: Towards noon Marianne's pulse slows and she sleeps quietly, and Mr Harris says that she has turned the corner.

beats.scene: Elinor leans over the bed with tears of relief on her face
beats.summary: Elinor finds the fever lower, and she begins to hope, though she is afraid to trust her joy.

beats.scene: Wheels crunch on the gravel at night outside Cleveland
beats.summary: That evening Elinor hears a carriage and, thinking that it is her mother, runs to the door.

beats.scene: Willoughby stands in a dark doorway, rain on his coat, speaking to Elinor
beats.summary: To her horror it is Willoughby who stands there, wet and pale, asking after Marianne, because he has heard that she is dying.

beats.scene: Willoughby faces Elinor in the drawing room with a haggard face
beats.summary: Elinor tells him sharply that Marianne is better, and he insists on explaining himself, so she lets him speak.

beats.scene: Willoughby speaks with his head bowed beside the dying fire
beats.summary: Willoughby admits that he first meant only to amuse himself, but that Marianne's love gradually won his own heart.

beats.scene: Willoughby clasps his hands and stares at the floor, unhappy
beats.summary: He says that his debts and his love of luxury made him ask for the fortune he needed.

beats.scene: Willoughby puts a hand over his eyes in the dim room
beats.summary: Mrs Smith heard about poor Eliza and turned him out of Allenham, and so he decided to marry Miss Grey.

beats.scene: Willoughby covers his face with his hands, remembering old letters
beats.summary: He says that he copied the cold letter from words that Miss Grey dictated, and that reading Marianne's letters nearly broke his heart.

beats.scene: Elinor looks at him sadly across the room, her arms folded
beats.summary: Elinor is moved to pity him, though she tells him that he has behaved badly and that he must leave.

beats.scene: Willoughby bows low and walks to the door, his shoulders bent
beats.summary: Willoughby asks Elinor to tell Marianne that he is sorry and that he will never be happy, and then he goes out.

beats.scene: Elinor sits alone in the drawing room, listening to the clock
beats.summary: Elinor sits alone and thinks over his story, ashamed of how much she pities him, and then hears wheels on the gravel.

beats.scene: A carriage rolls up as Mrs Dashwood steps out with arms wide
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood arrives with Colonel Brandon, and Elinor runs into her arms with tears of joy and tells her that Marianne will recover.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood kneels beside Marianne's bed, holding her thin hand
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood sits by Marianne, who wakes, smiles weakly and knows her mother at last.

beats.scene: Sunshine pours in at the window of the sickroom at Cleveland
beats.summary: Day by day Marianne grows stronger, and Mrs Dashwood hears from Elinor everything that has happened in London.

beats.scene: Elinor and Mrs Dashwood talk quietly by the fire after dark
beats.summary: Elinor tells her mother about Willoughby's midnight visit, and also about the long secret of Edward and Lucy, and Mrs Dashwood is both moved and angry.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon sits beside Mrs Dashwood, speaking gently
beats.summary: The Colonel tells Mrs Dashwood how deeply he loves Marianne, and Mrs Dashwood promises to remember his goodness.

beats.scene: Marianne walks slowly across the room, leaning on her mother's arm
beats.summary: Marianne can sit up and then walk, and Mrs Jennings, who is delighted, gives her every sweet she can find.

beats.scene: Marianne and Elinor walk slowly on a sunny hill, speaking earnestly
beats.summary: Marianne asks Elinor to tell her about Willoughby's visit, and she weeps but listens carefully.

beats.scene: Marianne sits very still as Elinor finishes the story
beats.summary: Marianne sees how wrong her own behaviour has been, and she grieves that she nearly killed herself with her own sorrow.

beats.scene: A carriage rolls along a country road with the Colonel riding beside it
beats.summary: At last they leave Cleveland and go home to Devonshire in Colonel Brandon's carriage, and he stops to bid them farewell.

beats.scene: Marianne stands at the garden gate of Barton Cottage in the evening light
beats.summary: Marianne walks round the little garden and weeps at the memory of the happy days with Willoughby, but then she smiles.

beats.scene: The family sit in the sunny room at Barton Cottage with books and music
beats.summary: At Barton Cottage again, Marianne resolves to read, study and be calmer, and she thanks Elinor for her care.

beats.scene: Elinor and Marianne walk side by side in the garden, laughing a little
beats.summary: The days at Barton are peaceful, and Marianne's cheeks begin to glow again as she reads and practises her music.

beats.scene: Margaret runs into the garden, waving her arms and calling
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood worries about Elinor, who is quiet and often thinks of Edward when she believes that nobody sees.

beats.scene: Thomas the servant stands at the cottage door, his hat in his hands
beats.summary: Thomas returns from Exeter and says that he has met Mr Ferrars and the former Miss Steele, who are now married.

beats.scene: Elinor sits pale at the table, hiding her face in her handkerchief
beats.summary: Elinor is stunned by the news and, though she tries not to cry, she weeps in her room for a long time.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood holds Elinor's hands in the dim room
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood, who knows Elinor's secret now, comforts her without a word, and wishes she had seen the sorrow earlier.

beats.scene: Marianne sits beside Elinor with a book unopened on her lap
beats.summary: Marianne tells Elinor that she is proud of her patience and prays that nothing so sad will happen again.

beats.scene: A tall pale man steps down from a horse at the cottage gate
beats.summary: A few days later a rider comes to the gate, and Elinor sees, to her astonishment, that it is Edward himself.

beats.scene: Edward stands awkward in the little sitting room, turning his hat
beats.summary: Edward is shy and quiet, and the family receive him politely but with surprise and embarrassment.

beats.scene: Edward says a few words and the whole family turn to look at him
beats.summary: Edward says that he is not married to Lucy, but Lucy Steele is married to his brother Robert instead.

beats.scene: Elinor runs from the room, weeping with joy and shock
beats.summary: Elinor rushes out of the room in tears of mixed relief, and the family are left looking at each other.

beats.scene: Edward kneels beside Elinor and speaks earnestly in the little parlour
beats.summary: Edward explains how Lucy chose Robert, now the rich son, and that he himself is free, and he asks Elinor to marry him.

beats.scene: Elinor smiles through her tears, nodding as Edward holds her hand
beats.summary: Elinor accepts him with tears of happiness, and he tells her that he loved her from the first week.

beats.scene: Mrs Dashwood hugs Edward and Elinor in the sitting room, laughing and crying
beats.summary: Mrs Dashwood is overjoyed, and Edward explains that he will be ordained and live at Delaford.

beats.scene: Mrs Ferrars sits stiffly as Edward bows before her in a grand room
beats.summary: Mrs Ferrars forgives Edward in time and gives him ten thousand pounds, so that he and Elinor can marry.

beats.scene: Edward and Elinor stand outside a pretty parsonage with roses at the door
beats.summary: Edward and Elinor marry and settle at Delaford parsonage, which they find very comfortable.

beats.scene: Colonel Brandon sits with Marianne in the garden, reading to her gently
beats.summary: Colonel Brandon comes to Barton often, and, little by little, Marianne begins to value his goodness.

beats.scene: Marianne smiles at the Colonel across a bright sunny room
beats.summary: Marianne at last sees that the Colonel's steady kindness is worth more than all of Willoughby's charm.

beats.scene: Willoughby stands alone at a window in a London house, looking out
beats.summary: Willoughby is unhappy with his rich wife and regrets losing Marianne all his life.

beats.scene: Marianne and Colonel Brandon stand before the altar at Delaford church
beats.summary: Marianne, at nineteen, marries Colonel Brandon, to her own surprise, and becomes the pride of Delaford.

beats.scene: Two sisters walk together through the green gardens between two houses
beats.summary: Both sisters live happily near one another at Delaford, and Elinor and Marianne remain close friends all their lives.

A1A2: The Dashwoods had lived at Norland Park in Sussex for many years.
Norland would go to little Harry, not to Henry's three daughters.
Henry became ill, and he asked his son John for help.
After the funeral, John decided to give his sisters some money.
His wife Fanny was shocked and said they could not afford it.
Fanny talked, and the three thousand pounds became much less.
In the end, John agreed to give them only small gifts.
Fanny came to Norland with her son and took charge.
Mrs Dashwood wanted to leave at once, but Elinor asked her to wait.
Elinor was calm and wise, Marianne was passionate, and Margaret was cheerful.
Fanny's brother Edward visited, and Mrs Dashwood liked him at once.
Edward and Elinor walked and talked, and they became good friends.
Marianne said Edward was too cold, but Elinor did not agree.
Edward told Elinor he wanted a quiet life, not a famous one.
Mrs Dashwood hoped Elinor and Edward would marry, but Elinor was careful.
Fanny said her mother wanted Edward to marry a rich lady.
A letter came from Sir John Middleton, who offered them a cottage.
Elinor thought Devon was far away, but her mother said yes.
Mrs Dashwood sold her carriage and packed her books and piano.
Marianne said goodbye to the trees and wept for Norland.
They travelled for several days to reach Devonshire.
Barton Cottage was small, but the valley around it was lovely.
Mrs Dashwood loved the cottage and planned new rooms for it.
Sir John Middleton came to welcome them with fruit and game.
At Barton Park, they met Lady Middleton and loud Mrs Jennings.
Lady Middleton's children were noisy, and she smiled at everything.
At Barton Park they also met Colonel Brandon, a quiet man.
Marianne said the Colonel was too old to fall in love.
Mrs Jennings joked that Marianne had won the Colonel's heart.
Marianne loved the wild hills above the cottage and walked there often.
Marianne and Margaret climbed the hill, though dark clouds were coming.
Rain fell, and Marianne slipped and hurt her ankle on the hill.
The man picked her up and carried her down to the cottage.
He said his name was Willoughby, and he would visit tomorrow.
Sir John said Willoughby was a fine young man and rich.
Willoughby visited, and he and Marianne loved the same books.
Elinor watched them and thought they spoke too freely.
At a small dance, Willoughby danced mostly with Marianne.
Willoughby and Marianne laughed about the Colonel, but Elinor defended him.
Marianne said no one can love twice, and the Colonel looked sad.
Willoughby asked for a lock of Marianne's hair, and she gave it.
Elinor worried they were not promised, but Mrs Dashwood trusted them.
Willoughby offered Marianne a horse, but they could not keep it.
Willoughby said he loved the cottage and wanted no change.
The Colonel read a letter and left for London at once.
Mrs Jennings guessed the letter was about a Miss Williams.
Instead, Willoughby took Marianne for a drive in his carriage.
Marianne and Willoughby went into Allenham while its owner was out.
Marianne laughed at Elinor and said true feeling was never wrong.
Willoughby read to the family each night, and Marianne loved it.
Willoughby came in, pale and upset, with sad news.
He rode away, and Marianne wept at the door.
Mrs Dashwood thought Mrs Smith wanted to separate the two.
Marianne would not eat, and she walked alone on the hills.
After a week, Edward arrived, but he seemed sad and quiet.
Marianne saw a ring with hair in it on Edward's finger.
Mrs Dashwood told Edward to be his own master, but he said no.
Edward left after a week, and Elinor hid her sadness.
Elinor kept busy, and she tried not to hope too much.
Mrs Jennings teased Elinor, and Margaret said his name was Ferrars.
Mrs Palmer laughed at everything, but her husband was rude.
Mrs Palmer asked the sisters to visit her at Cleveland.
Two cousins, Lucy and Anne Steele, came to Barton Park.
Lucy praised the children, and she wanted to be Elinor's friend.
Anne joked about Elinor's sweetheart, and Lucy asked about Mrs Ferrars.
Lucy told Elinor she had been engaged to Edward for four years.
Lucy showed a letter from Edward, and Elinor knew his writing.
Elinor kept her face still and promised to keep the secret.
That night, Elinor understood why Edward had been so sad.
Lucy talked of the secret again, but Elinor stopped her.
Mrs Jennings asked the sisters to stay with her in London.
Mrs Dashwood told her daughters to go, and Elinor agreed.
The sisters travelled to London with Mrs Jennings in her carriage.
Mrs Jennings's London house was big, and Marianne waited for a knock.
Marianne wrote to Willoughby again and again, but he did not answer.
Elinor asked Marianne if she was engaged, and Marianne said no.
Colonel Brandon visited, and he asked about Marianne and Willoughby.
They found Willoughby's card on the table, and Marianne cried out.
Mrs Palmer visited and laughed, but Marianne waited at the window.
Lady Middleton planned a party, and Marianne hoped to see Willoughby.
At the party, Marianne looked at every face for Willoughby.
Then Willoughby came in with a young woman and turned away.
Marianne called his name, but he spoke to her coldly.
Marianne felt ill, and Elinor took her out of the room.
The Colonel saw her pain and quietly brought the carriage.
That night, Marianne wrote to Willoughby again and waited all morning.
At last a letter came, and Marianne opened it with shaking hands.
Willoughby sent back her letters and said he loved another woman.
Mrs Jennings was kind to Marianne, but her loud words hurt.
Mrs Jennings told Elinor that Willoughby would marry a rich girl.
The next morning, Colonel Brandon asked to speak to Elinor alone.
He said Marianne was like a girl he had loved, called Eliza.
Eliza had to marry his older brother, and the Colonel went abroad.
Her marriage was unhappy, and she died poor and ill.
Before she died, she asked him to look after her little girl.
The girl grew up pretty, but at sixteen she went away.
Months later, the Colonel found her alone with a baby.
The man who had hurt her was Willoughby, and they fought.
The Colonel asked Elinor to tell Marianne the truth about Willoughby.
Elinor told Marianne everything, and Marianne listened and thanked the Colonel.
John Dashwood came to London and was very kind to Elinor.
John said that Marianne should marry Colonel Brandon, who was rich.
John took Elinor to a famous shop to buy a gift.
In the shop, a young man was choosing a small case.
He was Robert Ferrars, and he took a very long time.
Robert hardly looked at Elinor and laughed about small cottages.
Fanny asked Lucy and Anne Steele to stay at her house.
Fanny and Lady Middleton became friends, because both were cold and proud.
Fanny asked the sisters to dinner, and Mrs Ferrars was coming.
Elinor was afraid to meet Edward's mother and could not sleep.
At dinner, Elinor met Mrs Ferrars, who looked at her coldly.
Fanny showed Elinor's painted screens, but Mrs Ferrars liked Miss Morton's more.
Mrs Ferrars was kind to Lucy, and Elinor felt very sad.
Lucy whispered that Mrs Ferrars was being so kind to her.
Marianne was unhappy and rude, but Elinor hid her own pain.
A few days later, Edward came to see the sisters.
Lucy was in the room, and Edward went red.
Marianne greeted Edward warmly and asked why he looked so sad.
Edward left after a few minutes, and Elinor was proud of him.
Elinor knew that he had to keep his promise to Lucy.
Anne Steele thought Fanny knew, and she told her the secret.
Fanny cried loudly, and her husband John was shocked.
John ran to Elinor and told her the terrible news.
Mrs Ferrars came in a rage and sent the Steele sisters away.
Mrs Jennings heard the story and was full of excitement.
Edward kept his promise to Lucy, so his mother sent him away.
Elinor listened to every word, and Mrs Jennings did not guess.
Marianne learned that Elinor had known the secret for months.
Marianne felt ashamed of how she had thought only of herself.
Elinor said she was silent to protect others, and they hugged.
Colonel Brandon heard about Edward and wanted to help him.
He offered Edward a good church at Delaford, and Elinor was moved.
Elinor told Edward about the offer, and he said yes.
Edward said he could marry Lucy now, and he thanked Elinor.
John thought the Colonel's gift was a very strange act.
Elinor told Marianne that Willoughby had married Miss Grey.
Elinor wrote home, and her mother said they should come back.
Mrs Jennings said they could stop at Cleveland on the way.
Colonel Brandon said goodbye to Marianne, and she thanked him warmly.
The sisters left London and rode towards Somerset.
They reached Cleveland, a large house, and Mrs Palmer welcomed them.
Marianne learned that Willoughby's land was only a few miles away.
At dusk, Marianne walked alone in the wet garden.
She came in with wet shoes, and she looked very cold.
In the morning, Marianne had a headache and a high fever.
Mr Harris said she had a fever and must rest in bed.
Mrs Palmer took her baby and left, but Mrs Jennings stayed.
Elinor nursed her sister all day, and Mrs Jennings helped.
Marianne grew worse, and Elinor thought about writing to their mother.
At last Elinor wrote to her mother, and then she heard wheels.
The visitor was Colonel Brandon, and he was shocked to hear the news.
He said he would bring Mrs Dashwood in his own carriage.
He left at midnight, and Elinor went back to her sister.
Marianne cried out in her fever and called for her mother.
Elinor and Mrs Jennings watched together all through the long night.
Mr Harris saw no change, and Elinor began to lose hope.
Elinor prayed for her sister and remembered their happy childhood.
At noon Marianne slept quietly, and Mr Harris said she was better.
The fever was lower, but Elinor was afraid to feel glad.
That evening Elinor heard a carriage and ran to the door.
But it was Willoughby, wet and pale, asking about Marianne.
Elinor said Marianne was better, and she let him speak.
He said he had only wanted to enjoy himself at first.
He said he had debts and needed a lot of money.
Mrs Smith heard about Eliza and sent him away from Allenham.
He said Miss Grey told him what to write in the letter.
Elinor felt sorry for him, but she said he had done wrong.
He asked her to tell Marianne he was sorry, and then he left.
Elinor sat alone and thought, and then she heard wheels outside.
Mrs Dashwood arrived with the Colonel, and Elinor cried with joy.
Mrs Dashwood sat by Marianne, who woke and smiled at her.
Day by day, Marianne grew stronger, and her mother stayed with her.
Elinor told her mother about Willoughby's visit and Edward's secret.
The Colonel told Mrs Dashwood that he loved Marianne very much.
Marianne sat up, then walked, and Mrs Jennings gave her sweets.
Marianne asked about Willoughby's visit, and she cried, but she listened.
Marianne saw that she had been wrong, and she felt sorry.
They left Cleveland in the Colonel's carriage, and he said goodbye.
At Barton, Marianne walked in the garden and cried, and then smiled.
At home, Marianne decided to read, to learn and to be calm.
The days at Barton were peaceful, and Marianne grew stronger.
Mrs Dashwood saw that Elinor was quiet and often thought of Edward.
Thomas came back from Exeter and said Mr Ferrars was married.
Elinor heard this news and cried in her room for a long time.
Mrs Dashwood knew Elinor's secret, and she comforted her without a word.
Marianne told Elinor that she was proud of her patience.
A few days later, a man on a horse came to the gate.
It was Edward, and he was shy and quiet.
Edward said that he was not married to Lucy.
Elinor ran out of the room in tears, and the family stared.
Edward said Lucy chose Robert because he was rich, and he asked Elinor to marry him.
Elinor said yes with tears of joy, and Edward said he loved her.
Mrs Dashwood was glad, and Edward said he would work at Delaford.
After some time, Mrs Ferrars was kind again and gave Edward ten thousand pounds.
Edward and Elinor married and lived in the house at Delaford.
Colonel Brandon often came to Barton, and Marianne began to value him.
At last, Marianne saw that his kindness was worth more than charm.
Willoughby was unhappy with his rich wife, and he never forgot Marianne.
At nineteen, Marianne married Colonel Brandon, and she was happy.
The two sisters lived near each other at Delaford and stayed friends.
B1B2: The Dashwood family had lived at Norland Park in Sussex for many generations. Its old owner was a bachelor, and he was glad to have his nephew Henry's lively family in the house.
When the old man died, his will left Norland to Henry for life, and then to John and John's little son Harry. Henry's three daughters, who had hoped for more, were left only a thousand pounds each.
A year later Henry Dashwood fell gravely ill and knew that he would not live much longer. He sent for his son John and begged him to take care of the wife and three daughters he was leaving behind.

After the funeral John Dashwood was full of good intentions, and he walked alone in the garden to think. He decided to give each of his three half sisters a thousand pounds, which seemed to him a generous gift.
John told his wife Fanny of his plan, and she stared at him in horror. She asked how he could take so much money from their dear little Harry and give it away to his father's second family.

Little by little Fanny talked him down, first to fifteen hundred pounds, and then to a yearly payment of a hundred pounds. At last she argued that even this would be a burden, since the widow might live for many years.

Fanny pointed out that the Dashwood women would live comfortably on five hundred a year, with no carriage and few servants. In the end John agreed to give no money at all, only some help with their move and presents of fish and game.

A few days later Fanny arrived at Norland with her little boy and her servants, and she did not ask Mrs Dashwood's leave. She treated the house as her own, and the widow felt like a guest in her own home.
Mrs Dashwood was so hurt by Fanny's cold manner that she wanted to leave that same day. Elinor, who thought more calmly, begged her to wait until they had somewhere to go and the means to get there.

Elinor, who was nineteen, was calm, sensible and loyal, and she kept her strong feelings to herself. Marianne, three years younger, felt everything deeply and showed it all, while little Margaret was a cheerful girl of thirteen.
Fanny's brother, Edward Ferrars, came to stay at Norland, and Mrs Dashwood liked him at once. He was not handsome or bold, but his manner was gentle and his face was kind.
Edward and Elinor spent many hours together, walking in the park and talking quietly by the fire. She began to love his honest heart, though he was neither handsome nor bold.

One evening Edward read aloud, but he read the poetry without any feeling, and Marianne frowned across the room. She said that he had no passion, but Elinor answered that his good sense and kindness mattered more.
Edward told Elinor, in a low voice, that he longed for a quiet life as a clergyman. His proud mother wanted him to become a famous man, and he did not know how to refuse her.

Mrs Dashwood saw how close Elinor and Edward were becoming, and she hoped happily for a wedding. Elinor was more careful, and she reminded her mother that she could not be sure of Edward's feelings or of his mother's consent.
Fanny noticed the friendship and decided to put a stop to it. She told Mrs Dashwood, in her sharpest voice, that Mrs Ferrars expected Edward to marry a lady with a great fortune.
Soon a letter arrived from Mrs Dashwood's cousin, Sir John Middleton, who lived in Devonshire. He offered her a small cottage at Barton, close to his own house, for a very low rent.
Elinor thought that Devonshire was very far from Edward, but her mother was too eager to listen. She wrote back the same evening and accepted the cottage with warm thanks.
Mrs Dashwood sold her carriage and packed her china, linen and books, and Marianne's beloved piano went into a box. John said that he wished he could do more for them, but he did nothing.
Before they left, Mrs Dashwood invited Edward to visit them at Barton, and he promised to try. On the last morning Marianne stood under the old trees and cried, “Dear, dear Norland!”
The family travelled for several days, and Marianne was sad while her mother talked of the future. Margaret asked a hundred questions about the house, the hills and the neighbours.
Barton Cottage was small and plain, with only four bedrooms and two attics, and its roof was tiled. But the valley around it was green and lovely, and the hills rose high on every side.
Mrs Dashwood was delighted with the cottage, and she began at once to plan new rooms and a larger parlour. She had brought only three servants, but she said that they would manage very well.

The next day their cousin Sir John Middleton called at the cottage with a basket of fruit and game. He was a cheerful man of about forty, and he begged them to dine at Barton Park as soon as they could.
At Barton Park Sir John welcomed them warmly at the head of his table. They met his wife, Lady Middleton, who was cold and polite, and her mother, Mrs Jennings, who was loud, merry and eager to talk.
Lady Middleton talked about little except her noisy children, who were allowed to do whatever they liked. Elinor found the family kind but dull, and she hoped that she might find better company.
They also met Colonel Brandon, a grave, quiet man of thirty-five who was Sir John's close friend. When Marianne played the piano, he alone listened with real feeling while the others talked.

Marianne told Elinor that Colonel Brandon was far too old to feel love, and she added that he complained of rheumatism. Elinor smiled and answered that thirty-five was not so very old and that he was kind.
Mrs Jennings, who loved to arrange weddings, soon began to tease Marianne about the Colonel. The sisters bore it patiently, though Marianne found it very annoying.

The family settled into a quiet life, with Elinor drawing and Mrs Dashwood planning her garden. Marianne soon found that she loved the wild hills above the cottage, and she walked there almost every day.
One windy morning Marianne and Margaret decided to climb the high hill, although the clouds were dark. Elinor stayed at home with her mother, and the two girls set off laughing.
Soon the rain began to fall heavily, and the girls ran down the hill as fast as they could. Marianne tripped and fell, and she twisted her ankle so badly that she could not stand.
A young man with a gun and two dogs saw the accident and ran to help. He lifted Marianne in his arms and carried her down to the cottage, to the surprise of her mother and sister.
The young man said that his name was Willoughby and that he was staying at Allenham with an elderly relation. Before he left, he asked permission to call the next day to ask after Marianne's ankle.
Sir John told them that Willoughby was a lively sportsman who would inherit Allenham from rich old Mrs Smith. Mrs Jennings laughed and said that Marianne had set her cap at him.

Willoughby came the next day, and he and Marianne soon discovered that they loved the same poets. They enjoyed the same music and the same dances, and they talked as if they had known each other for years.
Elinor was glad that Marianne was happy, but she watched them quietly from her corner. She thought that the two of them spoke far too openly about everything they felt.

A few days later Sir John arranged a little dance at Barton Park, and Willoughby came early and stayed late. He danced almost every dance with Marianne, and some of the older guests looked on with disapproval.
Willoughby and Marianne joked that Colonel Brandon was dull and old-fashioned, and they laughed together. Elinor defended him sharply, saying that he was a man of knowledge, goodness and sense.
One evening Marianne said that nobody could ever love twice, and the Colonel looked at her sadly. Later he told Elinor that this opinion would not last, and she wondered what lay in his past.
One day Willoughby asked Marianne for a lock of her hair, and she let him cut it with a pair of scissors. She gave it as freely as if there were nothing to hide, though little Margaret was watching.
Margaret told Elinor what she had seen, and Elinor worried because there was no promise between the two. Mrs Dashwood answered that she trusted them both and did not wish to ask any questions.
Willoughby offered Marianne a fine horse as a gift, and she was delighted at the very idea. Elinor reminded her that they could not afford to feed it or to pay a groom.
When Mrs Dashwood spoke of building new rooms, Willoughby cried out that she must not change a single stone. He said that he loved the little house exactly as it was, and Marianne's eyes shone.
Sir John planned a picnic at Whitwell, and the guests gathered at Barton Park. But at breakfast Colonel Brandon read a letter, turned pale and left at once for London.
Mrs Jennings was sure that the letter concerned a young woman named Miss Williams, whom the Colonel looked after. The picnic was cancelled, and the guests went home disappointed.
Sir John, who was determined that the day should not be wasted, suggested a drive in the country. Willoughby offered Marianne a seat in his own open carriage, and they drove off alone.

When they returned, Marianne confessed that Willoughby had taken her through all the rooms of Allenham while Mrs Smith was out. Elinor felt a rush of disapproval, because she knew how people might talk.
Later Elinor told Marianne gently that such visits were improper and might be talked about. Marianne laughed and said that she had never behaved better, and that true feeling could never be wrong.
In the evenings Willoughby often read aloud to the family by the light of the fire. Marianne listened in delight, and Mrs Dashwood was sure that they would soon be married.
One morning Willoughby arrived at the cottage looking pale and unhappy. He said that Mrs Smith was sending him to London on business, and that he had to leave that very day.
He would not promise when he could come back, and he gave no clear reason for his hurry. Then he rode away, and Marianne, left alone, sobbed in the doorway.
Mrs Dashwood believed that Mrs Smith disliked Marianne and wanted to separate the two young people. Elinor was not sure, but she kept her doubts to herself.
Marianne gave herself up to sorrow, playing sad songs on the piano and walking alone on the hills. She would hardly eat, and she thought only of Willoughby.
About a week later Edward Ferrars arrived at the cottage without any warning, and Elinor's heart lifted. But Edward was very quiet and low in spirits, and he did not seem glad to be there.
Marianne noticed that Edward wore a ring with a lock of hair under glass. He said that the hair was his sister's, but he blushed, and Elinor hoped that it might be her own.
Mrs Dashwood told Edward that he should be his own master and stay as long as he liked. Edward answered sadly that he could not go against his mother's wishes.

After a week Edward rode away from the cottage, looking even more unhappy than when he had come. Elinor watched from the garden gate, and then she busied herself so that her mother would not see her tears.
While Marianne mourned openly, Elinor drew and read and taught Margaret, and she never complained. She told herself that Edward's heart was true, but that she must not hope too much.
At Barton Park Mrs Jennings and Sir John teased Elinor about her secret sweetheart and tried to guess his name. Margaret let the name Ferrars slip out, and Elinor felt her face grow warm.
Mrs Jennings's other daughter, Mrs Palmer, visited Barton Park with her husband. She laughed at everything and everyone, while Mr Palmer was rude and bored and read the newspaper.
Mrs Palmer begged the sisters to visit her home at Cleveland in Somerset, clapping her hands with joy. She also said that she knew of Willoughby, whose house was not far from her own.
Two poor cousins of Mrs Jennings, Lucy and Anne Steele, arrived at Barton Park for a long visit. Anne was older and rather silly, but Lucy was pretty and clever.
Lucy won over Lady Middleton by admiring her noisy children and praising everything they did. She also showed very clearly that she wished to be a close friend of Elinor.
Anne teased Elinor about her sweetheart Mr Ferrars, and Lucy asked a number of sharp questions about Fanny and Mrs Ferrars. Elinor was surprised that two strangers knew so much and cared so much.

While they sat apart from the others, Lucy told Elinor in a whisper that she had been secretly engaged to Edward Ferrars for four years. Elinor, who could hardly believe her ears, stared at her in shock.
Lucy proved her story with a letter in Edward's own handwriting and a small portrait of him. Elinor then understood that the ring Edward wore held a lock of Lucy's hair.
Elinor kept her face calm and said that she would never speak of it to anyone. Inside, her heart was breaking, but she let nobody see it.
That night Elinor sat alone and understood Edward's low spirits at last. She grieved silently, though she could not help pitying him for being trapped.
A few days later Lucy tried to speak of the secret again, hoping for Elinor's pity. Elinor answered calmly that she had given her word, and she gave Lucy nothing to enjoy.
Mrs Jennings was going to London for the winter, and she invited Elinor and Marianne to stay with her. Marianne accepted at once, hoping to see Willoughby there.
Mrs Dashwood pressed her daughters to accept, because she thought the change would help Marianne. Elinor had doubts, but she agreed to go so that Marianne would not go alone.
They travelled in Mrs Jennings's carriage and reached London after a long journey. Marianne said almost nothing on the way, because she was thinking only of Willoughby.
Mrs Jennings's house in Berkeley Street was large and comfortable, and the streets outside were full of noise. Marianne started at every knock on the door, hoping to hear Willoughby's voice.
Marianne wrote to Willoughby on the first evening and sent more letters in the days that followed. No answer came, and she grew paler every day.
Elinor asked Marianne whether she was engaged to Willoughby. Marianne answered that they had made no promise, but that she was sure of his love and needed none.
Colonel Brandon called at Berkeley Street and spoke quietly to Elinor. He asked her, with great concern, whether Marianne and Willoughby were engaged.
One day they came home from a drive and found Willoughby's card on the table. Marianne was overjoyed to learn that he had called, but he did not return.
The Palmers visited Berkeley Street, and Mrs Palmer's cheerful laughter filled the house. But nothing could comfort Marianne, who sat by the window every day and waited.
Lady Middleton planned an evening party in London, and she invited the sisters to come. Marianne dressed with trembling hands, hoping to see Willoughby among the guests.
The rooms at Lady Middleton's were bright and crowded, and Marianne searched every face as the guests arrived. Elinor held her arm and begged her to stay calm, but Marianne hardly heard her.
At last Willoughby walked in with a fashionable young woman on his arm. He saw Marianne across the room, and then he quickly turned his face away.
Marianne cried out his name and held out her hand to him. He came a few steps closer, asked coldly after her mother and then bowed and walked away.
Marianne's face went white, and she nearly fell into a chair. Elinor put an arm around her and led her out of the room while the strangers whispered behind them.
Colonel Brandon saw Marianne's face and understood everything without a word. He fetched the carriage quietly, and he did not trouble anyone with a question or a comment.
That night Marianne wrote to Willoughby again, begging him to explain what had happened. In the morning she sat by the window, and she watched every person who passed down the street.
At last a letter came, and Marianne tore it open with trembling hands. She read only a few lines, and then she threw it down and fell on her bed in tears.
Willoughby wrote that he was sorry to have misled her and that he was engaged to another woman. He sent back all her letters and the lock of hair that she had given him.
Mrs Jennings came in and comforted Marianne with great kindness and a plate of sweets. She meant well, but her loud sympathy only made Marianne's pain worse.
Mrs Jennings then told Elinor what all the town was saying about Willoughby. He was to marry Miss Grey, a young woman who had fifty thousand pounds.
The next morning Colonel Brandon called at Berkeley Street and asked to speak to Elinor alone. He said that he had something to tell her that might help her sister to heal.
He explained that Marianne reminded him of a girl he had once loved very dearly. Her name was Eliza, and she had grown up in his father's house as his father's ward.
Eliza's family forced her to marry the Colonel's elder brother, who did not love her. The Colonel, broken-hearted, was sent abroad to serve with the army and did not see her for years.
Her marriage failed, and she was shut away and left alone. When the Colonel found her at last she was poor and dying, and she begged him to look after her little daughter.
The Colonel placed the child, who was also called Eliza, in a good home in the country. She grew up pretty and trusting, and he hoped that she would be happy.

When she was sixteen the girl suddenly disappeared from the house where she lived. Months passed, and then the Colonel found her far away, alone and ill, with a baby in her arms and no one to help her.
The man who had ruined her was Willoughby, and he had left her without a penny. The Colonel challenged him to a duel, but fortunately nobody was hurt.

The Colonel explained that the letter at Whitwell had brought news of poor Eliza, which was why he had left so suddenly. He asked Elinor to tell Marianne the whole truth, so that she would stop grieving for a man who did not deserve it.
Elinor told Marianne the whole story, and Marianne listened in silence with wide eyes. Little by little she began to see Willoughby as he really was, and not as she had wished him to be.
Marianne ate a little that evening, and she thanked the Colonel with a trembling voice. She said that she would try to be calm, for her mother's sake and for Elinor's.
John Dashwood came to see his sisters in London, and he was polite and warm. He had heard that Mrs Jennings was rich, and he suddenly found her very agreeable.
John told Elinor that it would be a very fine thing if Marianne married Colonel Brandon. The Colonel, he said, had two thousand pounds a year and a lovely house.
A few days later John took Elinor to a famous jeweller's shop, because Fanny had asked him to buy something. It was called Gray's, and it was full of glittering things.
At Gray's they found a vain young man who was spending a very long time choosing a toothpick case. He picked up case after case and put each one down again, and he did not seem to notice anyone else.
The young man was Robert Ferrars, Edward's younger brother. He took about a quarter of an hour to decide, and at last he chose the most expensive case.
Robert hardly looked at Elinor, although John said who she was. Later he talked with a laugh about people who lived in tiny cottages, never guessing that he was talking to a girl from one.
Fanny, who knew nothing of Lucy's secret, invited the two Steele sisters to stay with her in Harley Street. She was so pleased with Lucy's flattery that she wanted her near her all day.
Fanny and Lady Middleton soon became good friends, because both of them were cold, polite and proud. They sat together for hours and agreed about everything.
Fanny then invited Elinor and Marianne to dinner in Harley Street. Elinor knew that Mrs Ferrars would be there, and her heart sank.
Elinor dreaded meeting Edward's mother, because she knew the cold way in which Mrs Ferrars thought of her. She wondered what the evening would do to her, and she slept badly that night.
At the dinner Elinor met Mrs Ferrars, a thin, upright woman with a proud face. She looked at Elinor coldly, and she did not hide the fact that she was not pleased to meet her.
Fanny showed Mrs Ferrars the little painted screens that Elinor had made. Mrs Ferrars glanced at them and said that Miss Morton painted much better.
Mrs Ferrars was very kind to Lucy, who flattered her cleverly and listened to every word. Elinor saw how cruel the situation was, and she could hardly keep her face still.
Lucy whispered to Elinor how very kind Mrs Ferrars was being, as if she were already one of the family. Elinor gave a small nod and said nothing at all.

Marianne was unhappy and rude at the dinner, and she answered questions with only a word or two. Elinor hid her own sadness so that nobody would guess it, and she tried to make up for her sister's manners.
Some days later Edward called at Mrs Jennings's house in Berkeley Street. He came into the drawing room and found Elinor, Marianne and Lucy sitting there together.
The meeting was very painful for everyone in the room. Edward blushed deeply, Lucy watched him with a satisfied look, and Elinor greeted him bravely as a friend.
Marianne greeted Edward warmly and wondered why he looked so low. She did not know the cause, and she thought that his mother must have been unkind to him again.
Edward stayed only a few minutes and then rose to leave. Although Elinor was very sorry for him, she admired the quiet way in which he had behaved.
Elinor told herself that Edward was bound to Lucy by his honour. She must keep her silence, and she must never let him see how much she suffered.

One morning in Harley Street Anne Steele believed that Fanny already knew about the engagement. She spoke of Lucy and Edward as sweethearts, and the dreadful secret was out before she realised her mistake.
Fanny fell into hysterics on the spot and screamed so loudly that the whole house heard. Her husband John, who had never been so shocked in his life, did not know what to do.
As soon as he could, John rushed to Berkeley Street to tell Elinor the terrible news. He was sure that she would share his anger, and he did not guess how long she had known.
Mrs Ferrars arrived at Harley Street in a fury and demanded to know the whole truth. She had the two Steele sisters driven from the house at once, and they left in tears with their boxes.
Mrs Jennings heard the whole story with great excitement and spoke of nothing else. She declared that Edward and Lucy deserved better treatment and that Mrs Ferrars was a cruel woman.
Edward was sent for and told to give up Lucy, but he refused to break his promise. His mother cut him off in anger and gave his inheritance to his younger brother Robert.
Elinor listened to every detail that Mrs Jennings gave her. The old woman did not guess how deeply Elinor felt it, and she thought her merely kind.
Marianne heard at last that Elinor had known of the engagement for four months. She was amazed that her sister had kept silent through all that time and had never said a word.
Marianne was ashamed of her own selfishness and told Elinor that she could never have borne such pain so quietly. She wept, and she asked her sister to forgive her for her neglect.
Elinor answered that she had not given way because it would have hurt other people. The two sisters held each other, and they were closer after that day than they had ever been before.
Colonel Brandon heard of Edward's trouble and wished to help him. He asked Elinor to offer Edward the living at Delaford, which was worth about two hundred pounds a year.
Elinor was moved by the Colonel's kindness and thanked him warmly. She wished, though, that the offer had come from someone else, for it hurt her to be the one to carry it.
Elinor went to Edward and told him of the Colonel's offer. Edward was humbled, and he accepted it with deep gratitude.
Edward said that with such a living he and Lucy could marry on a small income. He thanked Elinor for her kindness, and she felt her heart break a little more.
John said that Mrs Ferrars would never forgive Edward for this and that Fanny would be very angry. He thought that the Colonel's gift was a most strange act of charity.
A little later Elinor learned that Willoughby had married Miss Grey. She told Marianne gently, and Marianne bore the news quietly, which was a great relief to Elinor.
Elinor wrote home to say that they wished to leave London, and Mrs Dashwood's answer arrived within days. She said that her daughters should come home to Barton as soon as they could.
Mrs Jennings said that she would go with them as far as Cleveland, the Palmers' house in Somerset. They could rest there for a few days before they went on to Devonshire.
