Colonel Brandon came to say goodbye to Marianne and took her hand with deep feeling. She thanked him with a new warmth, and she called him her friend.
The sisters left London in Mrs Jennings's carriage on a cold, bright morning. Marianne looked forward to going home at last, and she hoped to find her peace again.
They reached Cleveland, a large and handsome house in Somerset. Mrs Palmer welcomed them with her new baby in her arms, and Mr Palmer greeted them with a yawn.
Marianne soon learned that Combe Magna, Willoughby's own estate, was only a few miles from Cleveland. Her heart ached, and she thought of him even in the pleasant garden.
One evening Marianne walked alone in the garden at dusk. The grass was wet after the rain, but she hardly felt the cold, because she was thinking of Willoughby.
She came in with wet shoes and stockings and said that she was quite well. Elinor saw that she was shivering, and she asked her to go to bed.
In the morning Marianne woke with a headache and a high temperature. Elinor sent for Mr Harris, the apothecary, who lived in the village.
Mr Harris said that it was a fever and that Marianne must stay in bed and rest. Elinor was frightened by his serious face, though he tried to speak lightly.
Mrs Palmer feared that the fever might spread to her baby, so she left at once with her child and her husband. Mrs Jennings stayed behind and promised to help in every way that she could.
Elinor nursed Marianne tirelessly, day and night, and hardly closed her eyes. Mrs Jennings, though loud and fond of gossip, proved herself a faithful and generous friend.
Marianne grew worse, and her skin was hot and dry. Elinor, who had never been so afraid, began to think that she must write to their mother.
At last Elinor decided that she must send for Mrs Dashwood, and she sat down to write the note. As she wrote, she heard the sound of a carriage at the door.
The visitor was Colonel Brandon, who had come to ask how Marianne was. He was shocked when Elinor told him how ill she had become.
The Colonel offered to fetch Mrs Dashwood himself in his own carriage. Elinor, who had not yet sent her note, thanked him with tears in her eyes.
He drove away at midnight, and Elinor went back to the sickroom. She felt thankful, but she was also very afraid.
Marianne raved in her fever and called out for her mother again and again. Elinor held her hot hand and spoke softly to her, although she did not know whether she was heard.
Mrs Jennings and Elinor kept watch together through the long night. Elinor learned how warm a heart lay under the old woman's chatter.
Mr Harris came again in the morning and said that he saw no change. Elinor's hope began to fade, and she looked at the clock and counted the hours.
Elinor prayed quietly for her sister and thought of all that they had shared since they were small. She remembered games in the garden at Norland, and she wept.
Towards noon Marianne's pulse slowed, and she fell into a quiet sleep. Mr Harris examined her and said that she had turned the corner.
Elinor found that the fever was lower, and she began to hope. She was afraid to trust her joy, because she had been so often disappointed.
That evening Elinor heard a carriage drive up to the house. Thinking that it was her mother, she ran to the door with her heart in her mouth.
To her horror it was Willoughby who stood there, wet and pale from his long ride. He had heard that Marianne was dying, and he had come to ask if it was true.
Elinor told him sharply that Marianne was better and that he should not have come. He insisted on explaining himself, and at last she let him speak.

Willoughby admitted that at first he had only wished to amuse himself with Marianne. Little by little, he said, her love had won his own heart, and he had been happier at Barton than anywhere in his life.
He said that his debts and his love of luxury had made him need a fortune. He had known for some time that he could not afford to marry a girl without money.
Mrs Smith had heard the story of poor Eliza and had turned him out of Allenham. After that, he said, he had decided to marry Miss Grey, who had the money that he needed.
He told Elinor that he had copied the cold letter from words that Miss Grey dictated. Reading Marianne's letters, he said, had nearly broken his heart.
Elinor was moved to pity him, although she told him plainly that he had behaved very badly. She said that he must leave the house now, because Marianne might wake.
Willoughby begged Elinor to tell Marianne that he was sorry and that he would never be happy. Then he turned and went out into the dark and wet night.
Elinor sat alone and thought over his story, ashamed of how much she pitied him. A few minutes later she heard the sound of wheels on the gravel.
Mrs Dashwood arrived in the Colonel's carriage, and Elinor ran into her arms with tears of joy. She told her mother, between kisses, that Marianne was out of danger and would recover.
Mrs Dashwood sat beside Marianne's bed and waited quietly. At last Marianne woke, smiled weakly and knew her mother at once.
Day by day Marianne grew stronger, and she began to eat and to speak. Mrs Dashwood stayed at Cleveland and heard from Elinor everything that had happened in London.
Elinor told her mother about Willoughby's midnight visit and about the long secret of Edward and Lucy. Mrs Dashwood was moved by the one and angry about the other.
The Colonel told Mrs Dashwood how deeply he loved Marianne, and he asked for nothing in return. Mrs Dashwood, who had grown to value his goodness, promised that she would remember it.
Marianne was soon able to sit up in a chair and then to walk across the room. Mrs Jennings was delighted and gave her every sweet that she could find.
One afternoon Marianne asked Elinor to tell her about Willoughby's visit. She wept as she listened, but she listened carefully and did not stop her.
Marianne saw how wrong her own behaviour had been, and she was sorry for it. She grieved that she had nearly killed herself with her own sorrow, and that she had caused her family so much pain.
At last they left Cleveland and went home to Devonshire in the Colonel's carriage. He rode with them part of the way and then stopped to bid them a kind farewell.
At Barton Marianne walked slowly round the little garden and wept at the memory of the happy days with Willoughby. But then she dried her eyes and smiled at the green hills.
Back in Barton Cottage Marianne decided to read, to study and to be calmer. She thanked Elinor warmly for her care and told her that she would never forget it.
The days at Barton were peaceful, and Marianne's cheeks began to glow again. She read for hours each morning and practised her music in the afternoon.
Mrs Dashwood worried about Elinor, who was quiet and tired. Elinor often thought of Edward when she believed that nobody was watching her.
One morning Thomas, the manservant, returned from Exeter with some news. He said that he had met Mr Ferrars there, with the lady who had been Miss Steele, and that they were now married.
Elinor was stunned by the news, and she tried hard not to cry in front of the others. When she was alone in her room she wept for a long time.
Mrs Dashwood, who now knew Elinor's secret, comforted her daughter without saying a word. She wished that she had seen the sorrow earlier, and she held Elinor close.
That evening Marianne told Elinor that she was proud of her patience. She said that she hoped nothing so sad would ever happen to her sister again.
A few days later a man on horseback rode up to the garden gate. Elinor looked out of the window and saw, to her astonishment, that it was Edward himself.
Edward came in looking shy and anxious, and he hardly knew where to look. The family received him politely, but with surprise and some embarrassment.
After an awkward silence Edward said that he was not married to Lucy Steele. Lucy, he told them, was now married to his brother Robert instead.
Elinor ran out of the room in tears of mixed relief and joy. The rest of the family were left looking at each other in amazement.
Edward explained that Lucy had chosen Robert, who was now the rich son. He himself was free at last, and he asked Elinor to marry him.
Elinor accepted with tears of happiness, and Edward told her that he had loved her since the first week at Norland. She said that she had hoped it, though she had never dared to believe it.
Mrs Dashwood was overjoyed when she heard the news. Edward told her that he would be ordained as a clergyman and live at Delaford, where he would work hard.
In time Mrs Ferrars forgave Edward, as proud women sometimes do when there is nothing else to be done. She gave him ten thousand pounds, so that he and Elinor could marry in comfort.
Edward and Elinor were married, and they settled at the parsonage in Delaford, which they found very comfortable. Their small house was always full of friends, and they were never in need.
Colonel Brandon came to Barton often during these months, and little by little Marianne began to value his goodness. She saw that he was patient, honest and kind, and she enjoyed his company.
At last Marianne saw that the Colonel's steady kindness was worth far more than all of Willoughby's charm. She understood that she had been wrong to ask for so much brightness and so little truth.
Willoughby was unhappy with his rich wife, who was cold and quick to anger. He regretted losing Marianne all his life, though he never said so to anyone.
Marianne, at nineteen, married Colonel Brandon, to her own surprise, and became the pride of Delaford. She gave him her whole heart, and she was a faithful and happy wife.

Both sisters lived happily near one another at Delaford, and their families visited often. Elinor and Marianne remained close friends all their lives, and they never forgot what they had suffered together.
C1C2: The Dashwoods had been settled in Sussex for many generations, and their estate of Norland Park was admired throughout the county for its fine woods and its comfortable, handsome house. Its late owner was an old bachelor who had lived quietly with his sister until her death left him lonely, and he then invited his nephew Henry Dashwood to bring his wife and daughters to live with him. In their cheerful company the old man discovered how much happier a house could be when it was full of young voices.

The old man's will brought bitter disappointment, for although Henry could keep Norland for his own lifetime, he could neither sell it nor leave any part of it to his wife and daughters. After Henry it was to pass to his son John and then to John's four-year-old boy, Harry, a child whom the old man had grown fond of for his little tricks and his charming ways. As a small kindness to the rest of the family, the will added a legacy of a thousand pounds for each of Henry's three daughters, which was very little to live on.

Henry Dashwood survived his uncle by only one year, and when a sudden illness left him weak and breathless he knew at once that he would not recover. He sent for his son John, the child of his first marriage, and from his bed he begged him, with all the earnestness he had left, to make his second family comfortable. John, who was not a cruel man, listened with real feeling and promised that he would do everything in his power.

When the funeral was over, John Dashwood strolled through the grounds of Norland, thinking with some satisfaction of his promise and of the generous way in which he meant to keep it. He had no wish to be remembered as a hard or ungrateful son, and he soon decided to give each of his three half sisters a thousand pounds, which would add three thousand to the little they already possessed. It seemed to him that he was being almost too kind, and he felt very warmly towards himself for it.

When John explained his plan to his wife Fanny, she was astonished and far from pleased, for she was a narrow-hearted, selfish woman with a great love of money. She reminded him that Harry was his only child, that every pound given to the Dashwood girls would be taken from the boy, and that no promise could oblige him to ruin his own son. John, who had never learned to argue with her, felt his generous plan begin to wobble.

Fanny was a patient and skilful arguer, and she did not give way in a single day. She reduced the three thousand pounds to fifteen hundred, and then, remarking that a gift of money is gone for ever, she proposed instead a yearly allowance of a hundred pounds, which she thought quite handsome. Even that, she said before long, would be a dreadful burden, for Mrs Dashwood was still young and healthy, and an annuity, once promised, can never be stopped.

She assured him that five hundred a year was a splendid income for four women who would keep no carriage, no horses and hardly any servants, and that they could never possibly spend so much. By the time she had finished, John had decided that he owed them no money at all. His promise, he felt, would be well kept by a little help with their move and a present of fish or game in season, and he went to bed thinking himself a very kind brother.

Within a few days Fanny arrived at Norland with her little boy and a train of servants, and she did not trouble to give the grieving household any warning. She walked in like a mistress who had at last come into her own, and nothing in her manner suggested that the widow was still the lady of the house. To Mrs Dashwood, who had been so recently bereaved, it felt like an insult delivered in perfect silence.

Mrs Dashwood was so wounded by this behaviour that she would have gathered her daughters and left Norland that very day, and she was prevented only by the tender good sense of her eldest girl. Elinor reminded her, in a gentle and steady voice, that they had no other home, very little money and no friends who could receive them, and that dignity would be better served by waiting than by running away. Mrs Dashwood, who felt every slight as violently as Marianne did, gave in with a sigh, though she did not forget.

The three Dashwood sisters were very different in temper, though they loved each other dearly. Elinor, at nineteen, possessed a calm judgment and a loyal heart, and she had learned to hide her strongest feelings for the sake of others. Marianne, three years younger, was generous, eager and romantic in everything, and she would no more conceal a sorrow than a joy, while thirteen-year-old Margaret already shared much of her spirit and little of Elinor's sense.

Soon afterwards Fanny's brother, Edward Ferrars, came to stay at Norland, and the widow, who had expected to dislike anyone connected with Fanny, was won over almost at once. He was not a handsome young man, and his shyness gave him a stiff and uncertain air, but his face was full of good nature and his manner was modest and sincere. Mrs Dashwood, who valued the heart above all things, decided that she had never met a more agreeable visitor.

Edward and Elinor were soon spending a good part of every day together, walking in the park, talking by the fire and discovering how much they thought alike. Elinor found in him an honesty and tenderness that she had never met in anyone else, and without ever deciding to do so she began to give him her heart. He was neither dashing nor eloquent, but she judged that a man of steady principles was worth far more than a man of fine speeches.

One evening Edward was asked to read aloud, and he read the poet's lines so calmly and so carelessly that Marianne, who could not bear to hear beautiful verses spoiled, could hardly sit still. She told Elinor afterwards that a man with no passion for poetry or painting would never understand a woman of feeling, and that she could not imagine loving such a person. Elinor replied gently that she did not need a lover who could recite, and that she greatly esteemed Edward's good sense and his kind heart.

One afternoon, sitting beside Elinor at the window, Edward confessed that he had no ambition for greatness, although both his mother and his sister wished him to rise in the world as an orator or a politician. What he really desired was a small house, a modest income and a quiet profession, and he thought the church would suit him best, although his mother considered it far beneath him. Elinor listened with growing tenderness, perceiving how much of his quiet unhappiness came from the weight of other people's expectations.

Mrs Dashwood watched the friendship between Elinor and Edward with growing delight, and she began to speak of a wedding as though it were already settled. Elinor, who had a cooler head than her mother, begged her to say less, because she could not be certain of Edward's heart and was still less sure that his proud mother would approve a girl without a fortune. Her mother only smiled and answered that love and merit would surely overcome every obstacle.

Fanny noticed the growing friendship and, determined to put an end to it, took Mrs Dashwood aside in the hall and informed her coldly that Edward's mother had very high hopes for him. She went on to say that Mrs Ferrars expected her son to marry a lady of great fortune and noble family, and that nothing must be allowed to interfere. Mrs Dashwood, deeply insulted that her daughter should be counted a danger, resolved to leave Norland as soon as she could find a house.

Before long a letter arrived from her cousin Sir John Middleton, a cheerful, generous gentleman who lived in Devonshire, and who had heard of her situation and wished to be of use. He offered a small cottage on his own estate at Barton, which he assured her could be made comfortable at a very low rent, and he urged her to accept it at once. Mrs Dashwood read the letter twice by candlelight, and for the first time in many weeks she felt her heart grow lighter.

Elinor privately thought that Devonshire was a very long way from Sussex, and from Edward, but her mother was in such haste to be gone that no objection could be heard. Mrs Dashwood sat down that same evening, wrote a warm reply to Sir John, and accepted the cottage with every expression of gratitude. Elinor, who had no wish to cast a shadow over her mother's new happiness, said nothing more and kept her own feelings to herself.

In the weeks before the move Mrs Dashwood sold her carriage, since she could no longer afford to keep one, and she packed her china, her linen and her books, together with Marianne's beloved piano. John Dashwood came to say that he wished he were able to do more for his stepmother, but that his own many expenses made it quite impossible just then. The hypocrisy of this little speech did not escape the sisters, though they were too well bred to remark on it.

Before the family left, Mrs Dashwood warmly invited Edward to visit them at Barton, and he said, with a shy flush, that he would come if he could. On the last morning Marianne wandered out beneath the old trees she loved and wept, crying aloud, “Dear, dear Norland, when shall I cease to regret you?” At the gate she turned for one more look at the house, and then the carriage door closed behind them.

The journey to Devonshire took several days, and as the carriage rolled slowly westward through unfamiliar villages and fields, each member of the family travelled in her own thoughts. Marianne sat in sorrowful silence, longing for the woods of Norland, while her mother spoke cheerfully of new gardens and new friends, and little Margaret asked a hundred questions that nobody could answer. Elinor, watching them all, felt that she alone was leaving the most precious part of her heart behind.

Barton Cottage stood at the head of a green and pleasant valley, and although it was small and plain, with only four bedrooms and two attics, it was neat and comfortable. A narrow passage led straight through it to the garden behind, with a sitting room on either side, and after the grandeur of Norland it seemed very humble indeed. Yet the hills rose beautifully on every side, and the newcomers, who were tired and anxious to be pleased, resolved to be happy there.

Mrs Dashwood, whose spirits could rise in an instant, declared herself delighted with the cottage and was soon planning how to enlarge it as soon as the family had a little more money. Their household was small, for she had brought only two maids and a manservant from Norland, and the rooms were far from grand. But she said that they would manage very well, because happiness had little to do with the size of a house, and even Marianne was at last persuaded to smile.

On the following morning their cousin and landlord, Sir John Middleton, appeared at the cottage door with a basket of fruit and a brace of pheasants, laughing and apologising for the plainness of the house. He was a good-looking, cheerful man of about forty who loved nothing better than company, and he insisted that they must come to dine at Barton Park as soon as they were settled. Mrs Dashwood, touched by such frank kindness, accepted gladly, though Marianne privately feared that his noisy good humour would prove tiresome.

At Barton Park, which stood quite close to the cottage, Sir John greeted them with such a hearty welcome at the head of his table that the strangers felt at home within minutes. His wife, Lady Middleton, was young, tall and elegant, but her politeness was cold and she had very little to say, while her mother, Mrs Jennings, was a fat, merry widow who laughed at everything. By the end of dinner Mrs Jennings had decided that she must find a husband for every one of the young Dashwoods.

Lady Middleton's conversation was almost wholly about her children, who were spoiled, noisy and quite uncontrolled, and who pulled at the ladies' ribbons and hair while their mother smiled and said that they were only high-spirited. Elinor and Marianne, who had been taught to value good manners and quiet conversation, found this very trying indeed. They could see that the Middletons were kind and sincere, but kindness alone, as Elinor thought, was a poor substitute for sense and taste.

Among the guests that evening was Colonel Brandon, Sir John's old friend, a grave and silent man of about five and thirty, whose manner was reserved but whose face was thoughtful and kind. When Marianne sat down at the piano and played, all the others talked noisily or admired her cleverness politely, but the Colonel alone listened with real and unfeigned feeling. Marianne, who had been hurt by the indifference of the rest, did not notice that the only person who understood her music was the one she was about to ridicule.

That night Marianne declared to Elinor that Colonel Brandon was quite beyond the age of romance, for a man of five and thirty had surely outlived every capacity for feeling and was fit only to be pitied. She added, with mock gravity, that he had complained of the rheumatism in his shoulder, which she took to be the commonest infirmity of declining life. Elinor, amused though not persuaded, replied that she thought five and thirty rather a young age for so grave a diagnosis.

Mrs Jennings, who had married off both her own daughters and now had little else to do, could not rest until she had found an admirer for each of her new friends. She decided almost at once that Colonel Brandon was in love with Marianne, and she teased the girl about it so often and so loudly that the poor Colonel looked uncomfortable and Marianne scarcely knew where to look. Elinor bore it with patience, reflecting that Mrs Jennings, for all her vulgarity, meant nothing but kindness.

Little by little the family settled into the rhythm of country life, with Mrs Dashwood planning her garden, Elinor sketching and teaching Margaret, and the evenings often spent at Barton Park. Marianne, who had been so sorrowful at leaving Norland, discovered that the high green hills above the cottage held a beauty of their own, and she took to wandering there for hours with the wind in her hair. It was a gentle beginning, though nobody could have guessed how soon it would be broken.

One windy autumn morning, in spite of heavy clouds that gathered over the valley, Marianne persuaded Margaret to climb the high hill behind the cottage and enjoy the wild weather. Elinor, who distrusted the sky, stayed at home with her mother and her sketching. The two girls set off laughing, their hair streaming in the wind, and neither gave a thought to the rain.

The rain came sooner and heavier than they had expected, and the two girls ran down the steep hillside as fast as their feet could carry them. Marianne, who was running faster than anyone, caught her foot on a stone, fell hard to the ground and found that she could not stand because of the pain in her ankle. At that moment a young man with a gun and two pointers, who happened to be shooting nearby, heard Margaret's cries and hurried to help.

Without waiting to be asked, the stranger took Marianne in his arms, carried her down the hill and through the garden gate, and did not set her down until he had reached the cottage sitting room. Mrs Dashwood and Elinor, who had been sitting quietly at their work, rose in astonishment at this sudden and dramatic entrance. Marianne, in spite of her pain and her wet clothes, noticed that her rescuer was extremely handsome.

He bowed, begged pardon for his intrusion and gave his name as Willoughby, explaining that he was staying at Allenham, the house of an elderly relation. Before leaving, he asked permission to call the next day to inquire after the injured ankle, and Mrs Dashwood, who was grateful beyond words, gave it at once. As he walked away through the rain he left a charming impression behind him, and Marianne's cheeks were redder than they had been all morning.

Sir John, who knew everyone in the county, told them with delight that Willoughby was the best shot and the boldest rider in the neighbourhood, and that he stood to inherit Allenham from a rich old lady. Mrs Jennings, who could not hear such a story without drawing a conclusion, laughed and said that Marianne had set her cap at him and had better take care. Marianne, though she pretended to be offended, secretly did not mind in the least.

Willoughby called at the cottage the next morning, and within an hour he and Marianne had discovered, with growing delight, that their tastes were the same in almost everything. They loved the same poets, played and sang the same songs, admired the same books, and they talked as eagerly as if they had known each other for many years. Mrs Dashwood, who watched them with a mother's pleasure, thought she had never seen her daughter so happy.

Elinor, who sat sewing in the corner of the room, was glad to see her sister so happy, but she could not help noticing that Marianne and Willoughby spoke their feelings with no reserve at all. They agreed with each other on every subject, praised and condemned the same people with the same delight, and thought nothing of showing in public what most people kept private. Marianne declared that reserve was only a disguise for coldness or for lack of feeling, and Elinor, who disagreed, said nothing.

Soon afterwards Sir John arranged a small dance at Barton Park, and Willoughby, who danced beautifully, came early and stayed late. He danced almost every dance with Marianne, they scarcely noticed anyone else in the room, and when they did separate for a single dance, both of them grew impatient to be together again. Some of the older guests looked on with raised eyebrows, but the young couple were far too happy to see them.

One evening Willoughby and Marianne amused themselves by making fun of Colonel Brandon, who sat sadly in a corner of the room and did not seem to hear a word. They declared that he was dull, old and cold, a man whom everyone praises and nobody remembers to talk to, and that he could never understand the finer feelings of the heart. Elinor, who could not bear such injustice, defended him warmly as a gentleman of sense, knowledge and real kindness.

On another evening Marianne declared, with the confidence of sixteen, that no one could truly love twice, and that a person who had lost a first love ought never to look for a second. Colonel Brandon, who had been listening quietly, took Elinor aside to the window and said, with a smile that did not hide his sadness, that her sister's opinion was one that time and experience would surely change. Elinor, who guessed that he spoke from his own past, wondered what sorrow lay behind his grave and gentle manner.

One morning Willoughby asked Marianne for a lock of her hair, and she allowed him to cut it off with a pair of small scissors, as freely as if there were nothing in the world to hide. Margaret, who had been peeping from the doorway, saw him place the lock carefully in his pocket-book and ran off at once to tell Elinor. The little girl was quite certain that anyone who had given and taken a lock of hair must be engaged.

Elinor, who did not like to hear her sister called engaged without any proof, spoke to her mother that evening and said that no promise seemed to have been made. Mrs Dashwood replied that she did not need to hear one, for a couple so open and affectionate hardly required to speak of their engagement aloud. Elinor, with a heavy heart, wondered whether such complete trust in two people so warm and so impulsive could really be wise.

Willoughby, who could not resist a generous gesture, offered Marianne a beautiful mare of his own breeding, and she accepted it with a joy that her mother found hard to resist. Elinor, who remembered what the others forgot, pointed out gently that the family could not afford a horse, a groom or the cost of feeding the animal. Marianne, with tears in her eyes, gave up the gift, and Willoughby said that he would keep the mare for her until she should have a home of her own.

When Mrs Dashwood spoke cheerfully of adding a new dining room and other improvements, Willoughby cried out in alarm that she must not change a single stone of the cottage that he loved so dearly. He declared that not one stone must be added to its walls and not one inch to its size, if his own feelings were to be regarded. Marianne, who listened with shining eyes, thought that no man had ever spoken so warmly.

Sir John had planned a pleasant day for the whole neighbourhood, a party to see Whitwell, a fine house and grounds some miles away, and the guests had gathered at Barton Park in high spirits. But at breakfast a letter was handed to Colonel Brandon, and as he read it his face changed, he rose abruptly and excused himself, and within minutes he was riding for London. Sir John, bewildered and dismayed, could only stare after him as every one of his careful plans fell to pieces.

Mrs Jennings, who loved a mystery, was sure that she knew what the letter concerned, and she whispered to anyone who would listen that it must be about a Miss Williams, a young woman whom the Colonel looked after. Sir John, thinking of his guests and his hampers, could only mutter that the Colonel must be a very odd man to go off in such a way. The picnic was given up, and the disappointed party broke up with many a sigh.

Sir John, who was determined that the day should not be wasted, proposed a drive in the neighbourhood instead, and the party set off in various carriages. Willoughby, who drove a light open carriage of his own, invited Marianne to sit beside him, and the two soon outdistanced everyone else. Elinor watched them vanish round a bend in the lane and wondered, with a small chill of unease, whether such freedom was quite wise.

When the couple returned, Marianne, glowing with excitement, confessed that Willoughby had shown her over every room of Allenham while Mrs Smith was out of the house. It was a fine old place, she said, and he had spoken of its future as though it might one day be hers. But Elinor, who knew what scandal could be made of such a visit, felt a rush of disapproval and could scarcely believe that her sister had been so careless.

That evening Elinor spoke to her sister alone and said, as kindly as she could, that such a visit was improper, and that unkind people might talk. Marianne, who thought the lecture absurd, replied with spirit that if there had been any impropriety she would have felt it herself, and that nothing done from true feeling could ever be wrong. Elinor, seeing that argument was useless, decided to be quiet and to hope that her sister's happiness would prove as lasting as it seemed.

As the autumn evenings grew longer, Willoughby formed the habit of reading aloud to the family by the light of the fire, and he read so beautifully that even Elinor was moved. Marianne sat close beside him, her eyes fixed on his face, and hung on every word as though no one else existed. Mrs Dashwood, looking on, was more than ever sure that a wedding would soon be announced, and her heart was full.

One morning, as the family sat at breakfast, Willoughby arrived at the cottage looking pale, distressed and unlike himself. He told them hurriedly that Mrs Smith had sent him to London on business, that he must leave that very day, and that he did not know when he could return. Marianne stared at him in dismay, and Mrs Dashwood, who had never seen him so shaken, begged him to explain.

Mrs Dashwood invited him to come back to them as soon as his business was done, but he only murmured that her kindness was too great, and that he could not say when he might return. Then, with a last look at Marianne, he hurried from the room and out of the gate, and was gone before anyone could ask another question. Marianne stood alone in the doorway, with tears running down her face, and wept as though her heart would break.

Mrs Dashwood, who always found the kindest explanation, decided that Mrs Smith disapproved of Marianne and had sent Willoughby away in order to part the lovers. Elinor was less certain, for she could not understand why Willoughby had not spoken of an engagement, and she wondered why he would not come back at once. Out of kindness to her mother and her sister, she kept her doubts to herself.

Marianne abandoned herself completely to grief, refusing to eat more than a mouthful, walking alone on the hills for hours and playing over and over all the songs that Willoughby had loved. She seemed to find a bitter pleasure in her own suffering, and she turned away from every attempt to comfort her. Elinor, watching her, thought that a little more control might have saved her sister much pain.

About a week later Edward Ferrars arrived at the cottage without any warning, and Elinor's heart leapt with a hope she had hardly dared to feel. But he was quiet and low in spirits, his greeting was cold and embarrassed, and he seemed more like a man who had been sent for than a lover who had hurried to see her. Elinor, hiding her disappointment as well as she could, asked kindly after his mother and sister and said nothing of her own feelings.

Marianne, whose sharp eyes missed nothing, noticed a ring on Edward's finger that held a plait of hair, and she asked him, teasing, whether it was his sister's, adding that she would have thought Fanny's hair darker. Edward answered with a blush and some confusion that it was, and then he fell silent. Elinor, who could not help hoping that it might be her own, was too gentle to press him, and the moment passed in embarrassment.

Mrs Dashwood, who liked him better each day and could not understand his restlessness, told Edward in the garden that he should be his own master and stay as long as he pleased. Edward answered, with a look of real unhappiness, that he was bound by duties and by his mother's wishes, and that it was not in his power to choose. Mrs Dashwood, puzzled, put it down to the proud and domineering nature of Mrs Ferrars.

At the end of a week Edward rode away from the cottage, looking even more unhappy than he had on the day he came, and Elinor stood at the garden gate until the last of him disappeared. Then she turned back to the house and busied herself at once with a hundred small tasks, determined that her mother should not see her disappointment. It was her habit to suffer in silence, and she had never needed the habit more.

While Marianne wept and wandered, Elinor, who felt a grief as sharp, took care to draw, to read and to teach little Margaret, and she never allowed her own sorrow to burden the household. She told herself that Edward's affection was certainly sincere, but that his mother's will and his own strange coldness made a happy ending unlikely. It was a sensible conclusion, though it did very little to comfort a heart that had been so ready to hope.

At Barton Park, Sir John and Mrs Jennings took a boisterous pleasure in teasing Elinor about a secret sweetheart and in guessing at his name. Margaret, who knew very well whom they meant and was eager to be clever, let the name Ferrars slip out before anyone could stop her. Elinor felt her cheeks burn at once, and Mrs Jennings, delighted with her success, roared with laughter across the table.

Mrs Jennings's other daughter, Charlotte Palmer, came to dine at Barton Park with her husband, and the neighbourhood soon learned that she was young, pretty and unable to stop laughing. She laughed at her mother, at the weather, at her own questions and at anything her husband said, however rude. Mr Palmer, a tall, grave young man who thought himself too clever for such company, hardly answered anyone and read his newspaper whenever he could.

Mrs Palmer begged the Dashwoods to visit her at Cleveland, her home in Somerset, clapping her hands with delight at the thought. She added that she had heard of Mr Willoughby, whose estate of Combe Magna lay not far from Cleveland, which made Marianne turn pale and then red. Mr Palmer, speaking at last from behind his newspaper, remarked that all such invitations were nonsense and that nobody ever wished to go.

Two new guests arrived at Barton Park that week, Lucy and Anne Steele, who were poor cousins of Mrs Jennings and had come to enjoy a long and pleasant visit at Sir John's expense. The elder, Anne, was a plain, talkative woman with little sense, but her sister Lucy was pretty, neatly dressed and wonderfully attentive to everyone. Sir John, who loved a crowd, was delighted to have two more girls to entertain.

Lucy made herself agreeable to everyone, and she won Lady Middleton's heart by petting her noisy children and admiring every one of their tricks, however tiresome. Elinor, who had little patience with such flattery, noticed that Lucy's smiles were quick and her eyes were quicker, and she thought her sharp rather than sincere. Yet Lucy turned her attention to Elinor with a persistence that was hard to avoid.

Anne, who had heard the gossip from Mrs Jennings, could not resist teasing Elinor about her sweetheart Mr Ferrars, and she laughed as though it were the finest joke in the world. Lucy said nothing, but listened with a strange and watchful interest, and later she asked Elinor a number of careful questions about Fanny Dashwood and about Mrs Ferrars. Elinor, who could not understand why a stranger should care, answered politely and was a little puzzled.

One evening, when the others were busy at cards, Lucy drew Elinor aside and told her in a low and trembling voice that she was bound to Edward Ferrars by a secret engagement that had lasted four years. She explained that they had met when Edward was studying with her uncle, Mr Pratt, near Plymouth, and that they had promised each other their hearts, though they had not dared to tell Edward's proud mother. Elinor, who felt as though the earth had moved beneath her, could hardly breathe.

Elinor, who could not at first believe it, was shown a letter in Edward's own hand, and when Lucy produced a small portrait of him as well, there was no room left for doubt. She remembered the ring on his finger, and at last she understood that the hair under its glass was not his sister's, but Lucy's. It was the cruellest moment of her life, and she bore it without letting a single feature change.

Elinor controlled her face and her voice so perfectly that Lucy, who had expected tears or anger, was visibly disappointed. She said gravely that the secret was safe, though she did not see why she had been trusted with it, and she wished Lucy every happiness. Then she returned to the card table and went on talking as if nothing had happened, while her heart was breaking.

That night, alone at her desk, Elinor went over every moment that she had spent with Edward and understood at last the reason for his silence and his troubled looks. She could not believe that he had loved Lucy, a woman so cunning and so poorly taught, but she knew that he would keep his promise to the end because he was a man of honour. She wept quietly for the first time, and in the morning she was calm again.

A few days later, as they walked together in the grounds of Barton Park, Lucy returned to the secret and spoke of her fears and her patience as though she expected praise for both. Elinor, who saw that she had been told in the hope of causing pain, answered with a calm and polite coldness that gave Lucy nothing. She resolved that she would neither complain nor betray the secret, whatever it cost her.

When Mrs Jennings announced that she was going to spend the winter in London, she turned to the Dashwood sisters with her usual warmth and pressed them to come and stay at her house. Marianne, whose face had been pale for weeks, accepted with a sudden brightness, for London was where Willoughby was, and she hoped to see him there. Elinor, who thought of the people she might meet in the city, was much less eager.

Mrs Dashwood, who thought that a change of scene would heal Marianne better than any medicine, urged both her daughters to accept, and she assured them that she and Margaret would be perfectly happy at the cottage. Elinor, who was uneasy about the whole plan, nevertheless agreed to go, because she could not let her impulsive sister be alone in a great city. The three of them spent the last evening together, and the next morning there was a great deal of kissing at the door.

The journey was a long one, and the carriage rolled through villages, market towns and wet winter fields while Mrs Jennings talked without pause about her grandchildren and her neighbours. Marianne sat silent in her corner, counting the miles and thinking of the one person she hoped to find at the end of them. Elinor, who listened politely to Mrs Jennings, looked out at the passing country and tried not to think at all.

Mrs Jennings's house in Berkeley Street was large, comfortable and full of the noise of the city, and the sisters were given a pleasant room upstairs, with a fine view of the busy street below. Marianne, who had hardly looked at the room, started up at every knock on the door and ran to the stairs at every footstep. Elinor, pretending not to notice, wrote a short letter to her mother to say that they had arrived safely.

Marianne wrote to Willoughby on the first evening, giving her address in a few trembling lines, and she sent two more letters in the days that followed. She waited at the window with an eagerness that was painful to watch, but there was no reply, and her lovely face grew paler and more anxious with every post. Elinor, who saw it all with growing alarm, dared not say aloud what she secretly feared about Willoughby.

On the third day Elinor asked Marianne gravely whether she was engaged to Willoughby, because her silence had begun to frighten her. Marianne replied, with some dignity, that she had no formal promise but that she was perfectly sure of his love, and that a woman who trusted her heart did not need any more. Elinor, who wished she could share this confidence, kissed her sister and said no more about it.

Colonel Brandon, who had come to London on his own business, called at Berkeley Street and asked to speak to Elinor alone, with an anxiety that he could not hide. He inquired earnestly, though he plainly dreaded the answer, whether her sister was engaged to Mr Willoughby, and Elinor replied honestly that she did not know. The Colonel sighed, wished Marianne every happiness and said, in a voice that she did not forget, that he hoped she would never be disappointed.

One afternoon, when they came home from a drive with Mrs Jennings, they found Willoughby's card lying on the table in the hall, and Marianne, with a cry of joy, snatched it up and kissed it. The servant said that the gentleman had called while they were out, and Marianne spent the evening in a delirium of hope and regret that she had missed him. But he did not call again that week, and her happiness turned into a fever of waiting.

Mrs Palmer, who had come to London for the season, visited Berkeley Street almost every day, and her cheerful laughter filled the drawing room while her husband yawned and looked at the ceiling. Marianne, who found such high spirits unbearable, sat by the window and watched the street, and she began to listen for the postman as for a footstep she loved. Elinor tried gently to talk to her, but she received nothing in return except a tired and distant silence.

At last Lady Middleton, who had arrived in town with her husband, arranged a large evening party, and the sisters were invited with Mrs Jennings. Marianne dressed for it with trembling fingers, took great care over her hair and ribbons and persuaded herself that Willoughby would surely be there. Elinor fastened the last pin of her gown and prayed that her sister's hope would not be broken.

The rooms at Lady Middleton's were bright with candles and crowded with strangers, and Marianne searched each new face with a hunger that she made no effort to hide. Elinor held her arm firmly and begged her to be calm, but the words fell on ears that were listening for a single voice. Every time the door opened, Marianne's whole body leaned towards it as a flower leans towards the light.

At last Willoughby walked in with a fashionable young woman on his arm, laughing at something that she had said, and he looked as handsome and at ease as ever. His eyes fell on Marianne across the room, and for one moment his face changed, as if he had been struck. Then he quickly turned away and began to speak to his companion, as though no such person had ever existed.

Marianne, forgetting every rule of polite behaviour, cried out his name in a voice that made heads turn and held out her hand to him with a look of anguished hope. He came a few steps closer, but he took her hand without warmth, inquired in a stiff voice after her mother and her sister and bowed. Then he walked away, leaving her standing like a person who had been robbed of all that she owned.

Marianne's face turned as white as paper, and her knees gave way so suddenly that she would have fallen if she had not sunk into the nearest chair. Elinor, who felt her own heart pounding with shame and rage, put an arm around her sister's waist and led her out of the crowded room. Behind them the guests whispered and stared, as people do when they have been given something to talk about.

Colonel Brandon, who had been standing quietly by the wall, saw Marianne's face and understood everything without being told a word. He slipped away without drawing anyone's attention, and he ordered the carriage to be brought to the door with the greatest speed. When it came he said nothing at all, for his kindness was of the kind that needs no thanks and makes no noise.

That night Marianne could not rest, and she sat up in her room writing a long letter to Willoughby in which she begged him to explain the cruel scene that she had witnessed. She did not sleep, and in the morning she took her place by the window and watched every person who passed along the street, with the patience of a prisoner who waits for a pardon. Elinor, who knew too well how this would end, said nothing and sat beside her.

At last a letter was brought in, and Marianne recognised the handwriting at once and tore the seal open with fingers that shook so badly that she could hardly hold the page. She read only a few lines, and then she threw it from her with a cry and flung herself upon the bed, where she wept with such abandon that her sister was frightened. Elinor picked up the crumpled letter from the floor with a heavy heart and read it through to the bitter end.

Willoughby wrote in cold, formal phrases that he regretted having misled her, that he had never meant to give her false hopes and that he was now engaged to another lady. He enclosed every letter she had ever sent him and the lock of hair that she had given him in the happy days at Barton. Elinor, reading the neat lines, felt contempt for a man who could break a heart and still keep his penmanship so steady.

Mrs Jennings, who had been told what had happened by Elinor, came into the room with a plate of sweets, a glass of old wine and a flood of loud and well-meant sympathy. She called Willoughby a scoundrel, a rogue and a villain, she pressed the sweets upon Marianne and she promised that the whole town would turn its back on him. She meant it all for kindness, but every word fell on Marianne's wound like salt.

Later in the day Mrs Jennings, who always knew what the town was saying, told Elinor in a low voice that Willoughby was to be married within a month. The bride was a Miss Grey, a young woman of no great beauty but of fifty thousand pounds, which was an amount that Willoughby, with his debts and his tastes, could hardly refuse. Elinor listened in a silence full of pity for her sister and of anger on her behalf.

The next morning Colonel Brandon called at Berkeley Street at an early hour and asked, with a seriousness that alarmed her, if he might speak to Elinor alone. When Mrs Jennings had tactfully left the room he told her that he had a story to tell, one that he had never told to anyone, and that he hoped it might help to heal her sister's sorrow. Elinor, who saw how much it cost him, gave him her full attention and waited.

He began by explaining that Marianne reminded him strongly of a girl whom he had loved when he was very young, in a way that he could never forget. She was called Eliza, and she had grown up in his father's house as his father's ward, so that they had spent their childhood days together and loved each other as naturally as they breathed. She had the same warm spirit, the same open heart and the same hatred of coldness that he saw in Marianne.

Eliza's family had other plans for her fortune, and they forced her to marry the Colonel's elder brother, a man who valued her money and not her heart. The Colonel, who was then a young man with nothing to offer her, was heartbroken and was soon sent abroad to serve in the army, where he spent many years in a state of numb sorrow. When he came home he learned that the marriage had been miserable and that she had been shut away after a divorce.

The marriage failed, and in the end Eliza was cast off and left to fall from one wretched situation to another, until her health and her fortune were both quite gone. When the Colonel found her at last she was poor and gravely ill, in a miserable lodging, and she was dying of a long illness that nobody had cared to heal. With her last strength she begged him to look after her little daughter, who bore her name and who was then only a small child.

The Colonel placed the child, who was also called Eliza, in a good home in the country, where she was kindly treated and well taught, and he paid for everything out of his own purse. As she grew up she became a pretty and trusting girl, with something of her mother's softness, and he hoped that her sad beginnings would be forgotten in a quiet life. He visited her as often as his duties allowed, and he told himself that he had at least kept his promise.

When the girl was sixteen she suddenly disappeared from the house in which she had been placed, and for months nobody could tell the Colonel where she had gone. He searched for her in every direction with a dread that grew worse as the weeks passed, and at last he found her far from home, alone, ill and ashamed, with a baby in her arms. She had no money, no friends and no hope, and she had not dared to write to him.

The man who had ruined her, and who had then left her without a penny, was none other than John Willoughby, who had been charming her at about the same time that he was charming half the county. The Colonel, in a rage that was quite unlike his usual calm, challenged him to a duel, and the two men met and fired, but fortunately nobody was hurt. He told this part of the story quietly and without any pride, and Elinor understood why he had always seemed so unhappy whenever Willoughby was mentioned.

The Colonel explained that the letter that had called him so suddenly away from the picnic at Whitwell had brought him news of poor Eliza's condition and of her desperate need. He said that he had kept silent for so long because the story was a shameful one, but that now Marianne's peace of mind mattered more than his own reserve. He begged Elinor to tell her sister the whole truth, so that she might stop grieving for a man who had never deserved her.

Elinor, who found it hard to say such painful things, told Marianne the whole story that same afternoon, while Marianne sat on the bed and listened in a stillness more alarming than tears. Her eyes grew wide, her hands closed slowly on her handkerchief, and little by little she began to see Willoughby as he truly was, and not as her own feelings had painted him. When it was over she was quiet for a long time, and Elinor, who watched her face, saw that something in it had changed for good.

That evening Marianne ate a little supper, which Elinor took for the first sign of hope, and then she asked that the Colonel be thanked for his kindness in a voice that was low but quite steady. She said that she would try to be calm, for her mother's sake and for Elinor's, and that she would not be so selfish as to waste more tears upon a man who was not worth them. It was a brave speech, and Elinor, who knew how much it cost her, kissed her without a word.

John Dashwood came to see his sisters in London, and he was so polite and warm that Elinor hardly knew him. The change was easy to explain, for he had heard that Mrs Jennings was a rich widow, and he now thought her a most agreeable and respectable woman. He praised the house, the dinner and the carriage, and he asked after his stepmother as if he had never forgotten her for a single day.

In the course of the visit John told Elinor, in a confidential tone, that it would be a very fine thing if Marianne should marry Colonel Brandon. He said that the Colonel had a large estate, about two thousand pounds a year, and no family to spend it, and that it would be a splendid match for a girl who had no fortune of her own. Elinor, who knew exactly how much generosity lay behind this opinion, answered him politely and said very little.

A few days later John took Elinor to a famous jeweller's shop, because Fanny had asked him to buy some small gift, and he did not trust his own taste. It was called Gray's, and it was full of glittering things in glass cases, which were guarded by a row of attentive shopmen in neat coats. Elinor, who had no money to spend, stood quietly beside her brother and looked at the sparkling trays.

At the counter they found a vain young man who was spending an astonishing time in choosing a toothpick case, and who seemed to think that the question was one of the gravest in the world. He turned over case after case, held each one to the light, put it down with a sigh and began again, and he never noticed the other customers who were waiting for their turn. When the shopman cleared his throat for the third time, he glanced at him with mild surprise.

The young man was Robert Ferrars, Edward's younger brother, though nobody at the counter knew it until John named him, and he took about a quarter of an hour to make up his mind. At last he chose the most elaborate and expensive case in the shop, and he left behind him a general sense of relief among the shopmen. Elinor, who had been watching him with a mixture of amusement and disbelief, thought that he and Edward could hardly have been born of the same mother.

Robert barely looked at Elinor, although John told him very clearly who she was, and he gave her only a careless bow. A day or two later, when they met again, he talked with a laugh about people who lived in tiny cottages, and he said that he could not imagine how anyone could bear them. He never suspected that he was speaking to a girl who had left a grand country house, and a rich brother's table, to live in one.

Fanny, who knew nothing of Lucy's secret, was so delighted with Lucy's flattery that she invited both Steele sisters to stay with her in Harley Street. She told her husband that she found Lucy the most agreeable girl in the world and that she wanted her always at her side. Poor Fanny, who was so careful in all her calculations, never dreamed that she was welcoming into her own house the very person whom she would soon be driving from it.

Fanny and Lady Middleton soon became the best of friends, because they were so exactly alike in everything that mattered. Both were cold, polite and proud, both had one child to adore and a great fear of vulgar people, and they sat together for hours in agreeable silence, finding nothing to disagree about. John and Sir John, who disliked each other quite as much as the ladies liked each other, took care to be in different rooms.

Fanny, who could not bear to leave her duty undone, invited Elinor and Marianne to dine in Harley Street, and she said with a pretty smile that her mother would be glad to meet them. Elinor knew very well that Mrs Ferrars would be there, and her heart sank, for she could not forget that the lady's cold eye would fall upon the girl whom she did not know to be her son's rival. She accepted the invitation for both of them with the best grace that she could find, and she tried to look pleased.

Elinor dreaded the thought of meeting Edward's mother, for she knew very well how a woman of that kind would judge a girl who had so little money, and she dreaded still more the thought of Lucy being there. She wondered what the evening would do to her, and whether she could keep her face as calm as she had promised herself, and she slept very badly on the night before the dinner. Marianne, who was no better, lay awake in the next room and thought only of Willoughby and of all that she had lost.

At the dinner in Harley Street Elinor was at last presented to Mrs Ferrars, a thin, upright little woman with a sour mouth and an air of settled disapproval. She looked at Elinor coldly from head to foot, and she made it perfectly plain, without saying a single rude word, that she did not wish to be pleased. Elinor, who was prepared for this, bowed and sat down, and she felt a strange calm as the dinner began.

After dinner Fanny, who was eager to display her sister-in-law's talents, brought out the little painted screens that Elinor had made, and she handed them to her mother with a flourish. Mrs Ferrars held them at arm's length, glanced at them for a moment and remarked, in the chill voice of one who has seen better work, that Miss Morton painted much better. Marianne, who thought the remark a gross insult to her sister, flushed with anger and answered rather sharply.

Mrs Ferrars, who was perfectly cold to Elinor, was kind and attentive to Lucy, who flattered her with great skill and listened to every opinion as if it were a verse of scripture. The girl sat beside her, praising the room, the dinner and the wise manners of her hostess, and Mrs Ferrars unbent so far as to smile. Elinor watched the scene with something like despair, for she saw how cruelly the joke of the situation was turning on her.

When Mrs Ferrars looked away for a moment, Lucy leaned towards Elinor and whispered, with great satisfaction, that she thought Mrs Ferrars was being most extraordinarily kind to her. She said it in a tone that suggested she was already a daughter of the family and that nothing at all could stand in her way. Elinor gave a small nod, which cost her more than an hour of ordinary effort, and said nothing.

Marianne, who had not the smallest wish to please anyone and who despised every person in the room, was unhappy and rude all evening, answering questions with a single cold word. Elinor, who saw it, hid her own sadness behind a calm face, for she knew that if she let it show she would only make her sister's manners seem worse. She tried to smile at the right moments and to speak when it was needed, and she felt very tired.

Some days later, in the middle of the morning, Edward called at Mrs Jennings's house in Berkeley Street, and the servant showed him into the drawing room with no warning at all. He found Elinor and Marianne sitting there with Lucy, who had come to pay a visit, and for a moment he stood in the doorway as though he wished the floor would swallow him. It was the very thing that Elinor had dreaded for weeks, and now that it had come she felt only a numb surprise.

The meeting was very painful, for Edward blushed to the roots of his hair, Lucy sat with her eyes fixed upon him, and the silence dragged on for what seemed an hour. Elinor, who had decided long before what she would do, rose bravely and greeted him as a friend, shook his hand and asked about his health and his mother's, in a voice that did not shake. Edward answered in a few confused words, and nobody in the room was deceived by his poor attempt at calm.

Marianne, who knew nothing of what had passed, greeted Edward with a warmth that was meant to cover her sister's coolness, and she asked him tenderly why he seemed so unhappy. She thought that his mother must have been unkind to him again, and she looked at him with the pity of one who had suffered a great deal herself. Edward, who dared not meet her eyes, said that he was perfectly well, and he looked at the floor.

Edward stayed only a few minutes, murmured something about an engagement and left the room in such confusion that he nearly forgot his hat. Elinor, who watched him go, felt a rush of pity for the man who had been caught in a net of his own youth, and she could not help admiring the quiet dignity with which he had borne it all. When the door closed behind him she sat very still, and her heart ached with a sorrow that she could not share.

When she was alone, Elinor reasoned with herself as she had so many times before, and she told herself that Edward was bound to Lucy by his honour and that he had never meant to deceive her. She must keep her silence, and she must never let him see how much she suffered, for to do so would only add another burden to his heavy load. It was a hard thing to feel and a harder thing to hide, but she had her mother and her sister to think of.

One morning in Harley Street Anne Steele, who had a great deal of curiosity and very little sense, fancied that Fanny already knew about the engagement, and she began to talk of Lucy and Edward as one speaks of sweethearts. She chattered on with an air of great confidence, mentioning their letters, their vows and their four long years of waiting, and she did not stop until she saw her hostess's face. By then the dreadful secret was out and nobody could possibly take it back.

Fanny fell into hysterics on the spot, and her screams were so loud and so long that the whole household heard them and the servants ran to the door. Her husband John, who had never been so shocked in his life and who had not the least idea of what to do, wrung his hands and called for salts and water and a doctor. Lucy, who sat pale and silent in a corner, said nothing, for she knew that the truth could not be mended.

As soon as his wife was able to be left, John rushed in great agitation to Berkeley Street, so that Elinor should hear the terrible news from his own lips and not from a stranger's. He was quite sure that she would share his outrage, and that she would see at once what a dreadful thing it was for Edward to wish to marry a girl without money or family. It never crossed his mind that the news was not new to her, nor that she had known it for months.

Mrs Ferrars, who had been sent for in haste, arrived at Harley Street in a perfect fury and demanded to be told the whole truth from beginning to end. When she had heard it she turned upon the Steele sisters and had them driven out of the house within the hour, and they were left standing in the street with their boxes and tears on their faces. It was a cold and savage scene, and Fanny, recovering at last, enjoyed it exceedingly.

Mrs Jennings, who had a weakness for gossip, heard the whole story with a joy that she made no effort to hide, and for the next few days she spoke of nothing else to anybody who would listen. She declared with great warmth that Edward and Lucy deserved much better treatment, that Mrs Ferrars was a hard and cruel woman, and that if she were Edward she would marry the girl tomorrow. Elinor sat quietly beside her, with her needlework in her lap, and heard every single word.

Edward was sent for in his turn and told to give up Lucy at once, and he refused, with perfect politeness and perfect firmness, to break the promise that he had made. His mother, who had expected to be obeyed at once, cut him off in a transport of anger, took away his inheritance and gave it all, with the family fortune, to his younger brother Robert. It was the harshest punishment that she could devise, and she was glad of it.

Elinor listened to every detail that Mrs Jennings could give her, and she asked a few quiet questions at the right moments, as any kind friend might. The old woman, who thought her merely sympathetic, did not guess for an instant how deeply it touched her, or why she looked so grave when Edward's name was spoken. Elinor, who had at last learned to hide everything behind a pleasant face, felt more alone than she had ever felt in her life.

In the course of a quiet evening Marianne learned that Elinor had known of Edward's engagement for four whole months, and she was astounded that her sister had kept silent through all that time. She had seen her sister's calm face on a hundred occasions and had thought it a sign of coldness, and now she saw what lay beneath. The discovery struck her like a blow, and she sat very still for a long while.

Marianne, who had been so occupied with her own grief that she had never thought of anyone else's, was ashamed of her selfishness and told Elinor that she could never have borne such pain so quietly. She wept, and she asked Elinor to forgive her for all the days on which she had been blind and unkind, and she said that she had thought her sister's patience a form of indifference. Elinor, deeply moved, did not say that she had sometimes wondered whether it was one.

Elinor answered that she had not given way because it would have hurt other people as well as herself, and she explained that a promise had bound her tongue and that she could not break it. She confessed that she had not been strong, only careful, and that she had wept many times in private, behind a closed door. The sisters held each other for a long while, and from that day forward their affection was deeper and more tender than before.

Colonel Brandon, who had heard of Edward's disgrace from Mrs Jennings, felt that a man should not suffer so severely for his honour, and he wished to be of use to him in some manner. He had a small church at Delaford which had lately become vacant, and he asked Elinor, with a diffidence that she found touching, to offer it to Edward. The living was worth about two hundred pounds a year, which he knew was little but which would at least provide a roof.

Elinor was deeply moved by the Colonel's kindness and thanked him with a warmth that surprised even herself, for she saw that he was a man who did good for its own sake. She felt, however, a certain bitterness at being the messenger of this particular gift, for it would help the man she loved to marry another woman. She wished that the offer had come from anyone but herself, and then she was ashamed of the wish.

Elinor went to Edward, who had come to see her in a state of low and gloomy resignation, and she told him of the Colonel's offer as simply as she could. Edward was so astonished and so humbled by it that for a long minute he could not speak, and then he accepted the living with a gratitude that did him credit. His eyes were fixed on the floor, and she knew that he was thinking of the future.

Edward said that with such a living he and Lucy might marry on a small income, if they were careful, and that it was the first piece of good fortune that he had had in a year. He thanked Elinor warmly for her kindness and said that he would never forget what he owed her. She listened and smiled, and with each word she felt her own heart break a little more.

John, who heard of the offer from Fanny, said in a tone of scandalised surprise that Mrs Ferrars would never forgive Edward for taking it and that Fanny would be furious. He thought that the Colonel's gift was a most strange act of charity, for who could give a living to a man whom his own family had cast off? He shook his head and was sure that there was something odd behind it.

A few days later Elinor, who had heard the rumour from Mrs Jennings and had found it to be true, learned that Willoughby had married Miss Grey. She told Marianne gently, bracing herself for another storm of tears, but Marianne bore the news quietly and said only that she hoped he would be happy. Elinor, who had feared a tempest, was so relieved that she could hardly speak.

Elinor wrote home to say that she and Marianne wished to leave London as soon as they could do so with decency, and Mrs Dashwood's answer arrived within a few days, full of love and relief. She said that her daughters should come back to Barton at once, and that she would be happy to have them under her own roof again. Elinor read the letter twice over, and Marianne, who was hungry for news of the cottage, read it three times.

Mrs Jennings, who was not at all offended, said that she would travel with them as far as Cleveland, the Palmers' fine house in Somerset, so that they might rest there before going on to Devonshire. She had promised her daughter a visit in any case, and she thought that country air would do Marianne a world of good. The sisters accepted gratefully, for they had no wish to be rude to so kind a friend, and they began to pack.

Colonel Brandon came on the last evening to say goodbye to Marianne, and he took her hand with a feeling that he did not try to disguise. Marianne, who for the first time in months looked at him with attention, thanked him for all that he had done and called him her friend, and she said it in a way that made him blush. The Colonel bowed over her hand, and for a long moment he could not find a single word to say.

The sisters left London in Mrs Jennings's carriage on a cold, bright morning, with the noise of the city fading behind them and the spring beginning to show in the hedges. Marianne looked out of the window with a calm that Elinor had not seen for months, and she looked forward to going home at last, to her mother and Margaret and the little house among the hills. Elinor, who had so many private cares, was glad to see her sister quiet.

They reached Cleveland, a large and handsome house in Somerset standing among lawns and shrubberies, and Mrs Palmer ran out to welcome them with her new baby in her arms and a stream of cheerful chatter. Her husband, who was following her, greeted them with a yawn and a nod, as though visitors were an inconvenience that he had long ago accepted. Mrs Jennings, delighted to be among her family, sat down at once and began to ask about everything.

Marianne soon learned, through some careless remark from Mrs Palmer, that Combe Magna, Willoughby's own estate, lay only a few miles from Cleveland, and she felt her heart contract as though the knowledge were a physical wound. She said nothing, but she began to wander by herself through the gardens and shrubberies and to look toward the horizon, where she supposed that the house must stand. Elinor, who saw her pale face and her restless eyes, watched her closely and said very little.

One evening, when the rain had stopped and the sky was clearing, Marianne walked alone in the garden at dusk and let her feet carry her wherever they pleased. The grass was soaked and the evening damp and cold, but she hardly noticed it, for her thoughts were far away and her feelings quite beyond the reach of common sense. She walked on, deaf to the call of the servants, until the first stars appeared.

She came in with wet shoes and stockings and said, with a smile that deceived nobody, that she was quite well and wanted nothing. Elinor, who noticed the heavy eyes and the heightened colour, saw that she was shivering, and she begged her to change at once and go straight to bed. Marianne yielded unwillingly and went upstairs, and Elinor, who stood and watched her go, felt a vague alarm that she could not explain.

In the morning Marianne woke with a violent headache and a burning temperature, and she could hardly lift her head from the pillow. Elinor, who had known her sister's constitution since they were small, sent at once for Mr Harris, the apothecary, who lived in the village and was thought to be a man of experience. Marianne lay with her eyes half closed and her cheeks flushed, and she did not appear to hear what was said.

Mr Harris examined her and said gravely that it was a fever, and that Marianne must stay in bed and rest, with plenty of cool drinks and no disturbance. He spoke with such a studied lightness that Elinor was frightened, for she knew from the care in his face that he thought the case serious. She thanked him, saw him to the door and returned to the sickroom with a heart that felt like lead.

Mrs Palmer, who was a good deal more frightened than she liked to show, feared that the fever might spread to her baby, and she left Cleveland that same day. Mrs Jennings, who was a good deal braver, said that she would not stir from the house while Marianne needed anyone, and she settled herself in as a nurse. Elinor, who had looked for no such kindness, was greatly touched, and she thanked her with tears in her eyes.

Elinor nursed her sister tirelessly, giving her the cooling drinks that Mr Harris had ordered, bathing her forehead and listening to her breathing at every hour of the night. Mrs Jennings, who was loud, fond of gossip and sometimes tiresome, proved herself in these days a faithful and generous friend, who thought nothing of her own comfort when another's was at stake. Elinor, who had once misjudged her, was very glad to find herself so entirely in the wrong.

Marianne grew worse with each day, and her skin was hot and dry, her eyes were wild and she no longer knew where she was or who sat beside her. Elinor, who had never in her life been so afraid, found that her thoughts kept running back to Barton Cottage, and she began to think that she must at last write to her mother. She was afraid of alarming her, and still more afraid of leaving it too late.

At last, after a night of terror, Elinor decided that she must send for Mrs Dashwood, and she sat down at the writing table with a shaking hand to compose the note. She had not written more than three lines, and she was struggling to find the right words, when she heard the sound of a carriage at the door. Her heart leapt, for she thought that it might be a messenger, and she rose with the pen still in her hand.

The visitor was Colonel Brandon, who had travelled from Delaford to ask how Marianne was, and he was so shocked when Elinor told him how ill she had become that he stood in the hall and could not speak. His face, always grave, grew grey, and he looked at her as if he had been struck by a hand. Elinor had never before seen such open pain on the face of any man.

The Colonel offered, with an eagerness that he could not conceal, to fetch Mrs Dashwood himself in his own carriage, since nobody else could reach Barton so quickly or so safely. Elinor, who had not yet had time to send her note and who saw at once how much good sense lay in the proposal, thanked him with tears in her eyes. It was plain to her that his heart was wholly engaged, and she liked him the better for it.

He drove away at midnight, into a night of wind and darkness, and Elinor watched the lamps of the carriage until they were gone and then went back to the sickroom. She felt thankful for his help, but she was also very afraid, for the hours that were to pass before her mother could arrive seemed as long as a year. Marianne lay still in the dim light, and Elinor sat beside the bed and listened to her breathing.

In the small hours Marianne began to rave in her fever, and she called out for her mother again and again, in a voice so full of longing that it cut Elinor to the heart. Elinor held her hot hand, spoke softly to her and bathed her forehead, although she did not know whether she was heard or understood. Every few minutes the sick girl turned her head restlessly and spoke the name of someone who was not there.

Mrs Jennings and Elinor kept watch together throughout the long night, taking turns to sit by the bed and to rest in the chair, and they spoke in whispers whenever they spoke at all. In those quiet hours Elinor learned how warm and true a heart lay beneath the old woman's loud chatter, and how much real tenderness she had for the sisters. She had been wrong to judge so good a woman by her manners alone, and she was glad to say so.

Mr Harris came again in the early morning, examined his patient with careful attention and said gravely that he saw no change, and that they must wait and hope. Elinor's own hope, which had been burning so low, began to fade, and she looked at the clock and counted the minutes as if each of them were a stone upon her heart. She did not cry, for she felt that she had no tears left to shed and no strength to spare for them.

Elinor prayed quietly for her sister, for there was nothing else that she could do, and as she prayed she thought of all that they had shared since they were small children. She remembered the games in the garden at Norland, the songs on the piano and the long walks in the woods, and she wept in silence, with her hand over her mouth. It seemed to her that nothing in the world could be worth the loss of Marianne.

Towards noon Marianne's pulse slowed and her breathing grew deeper, and she fell into a quiet sleep that was quite unlike the restless sleep of the day before. Mr Harris, who was called at once and who examined her with a look of growing satisfaction, said that she had turned the corner and that the danger was now much less. Elinor, who could not believe her ears, took his hand and thanked him in a trembling voice.

Elinor found that the fever was lower, that the burning of the skin had given way to a gentle warmth and that her sister's face looked calm for the first time in many days. She began to hope, but she was afraid to trust her joy, because she had been disappointed so many times in the course of that dreadful week. She sat beside the bed with her hand upon the coverlet and watched the breathing, and she dared not move.
