That evening, when the lamps were lit and the house had grown quiet, Elinor heard a carriage drive up to the front door, and her heart gave a great leap. Thinking that it must be her mother, who had been fetched at such speed and at such cost, she ran down the stairs and across the hall with her face alight. She flung open the door with both hands and stood there, breathless, in the light.

To her horror it was not her mother at all but Willoughby who stood in the doorway, wet through and pale as a ghost from his long and furious ride. He asked, in a hoarse voice, whether it was true that Marianne was dying, for he had heard it in London and had not stopped to rest. Elinor stepped back in dismay, and for a long moment she could not find a single word to say.

Elinor told him sharply that Marianne was better and that he should never have come, but he insisted with such passion on explaining himself that she could not refuse. She stood looking at him in the hall for some time, and at last she said, with a coldness she hardly felt, that he might speak for ten minutes and no longer. He bowed his head, took a long, unsteady breath and began his sorry tale, with his eyes on the floor and his hat in his hands.

Willoughby admitted without excuse that at first he had meant only to amuse himself with Marianne, and that he had been careless of the effect of his attentions. Little by little, he said, her love had won his own heart, and he had been happier at Barton than anywhere else in his whole life. Elinor listened with her arms folded and her face stern, and she did not interrupt him once.

He explained that his debts and his love of luxury had made him need a fortune, for he had been brought up to spend freely and had never learned to do without. He had known for some time that he could not afford to marry a girl without money, and he had put off the question rather than face it. It was a poor sort of defence, and he knew it better than anyone who stood there to hear it.

Mrs Smith, who had heard the whole story of poor Eliza from some well-wisher, had turned him out of Allenham with no money and no hope of any, and that disaster had decided everything. After that, he said, he had no choice but to marry Miss Grey, who had the money that he needed and who was willing to have him. He said it in the tone of a man who describes the death of a friend.

He told Elinor that the cold letter that Marianne had received had been copied by him from words that Miss Grey had dictated, and he said that reading Marianne's tender letters had nearly broken his heart. He confessed that he had not slept properly for three nights and that he had felt hateful to himself. He spoke quickly and without pause, like a man who is relieved to confess at last and who fears that his courage may fail before he has finished.

Elinor was moved to pity him in spite of herself, for there was a trace of real feeling in his face, but she told him plainly that he had behaved very badly. She said that he must leave the house now, since Marianne might wake and since he had no right to be there. Her voice was gentle, but her words were firm, and he understood that there was no appeal against them.

Willoughby begged Elinor to tell Marianne that he was sorry and that he would never be happy again, though he had chosen his own road and must walk it to the end. He bowed to her with a look of the deepest misery, and then he turned and went out into the wet and windy night. She heard his footsteps die away and was left staring at the empty doorway.

Elinor sat alone in the hall and thought over all that he had said, ashamed to find how much she pitied him and how little she wished to. Then, in the middle of her confusion, she heard the sound of wheels on the gravel, and the clatter of horses stopping at the door. She rose with a cry of hope, and this time she was not mistaken.

Mrs Dashwood stepped out of the Colonel's carriage, weary and white-faced after her long journey, and Elinor ran into her arms with tears of joy. She told her mother, between kisses and half-finished sentences, that Marianne was out of danger and that she would certainly recover. Behind them Colonel Brandon stood quietly in the lamplight, with a look that said more than words could have said.

Mrs Dashwood sat beside Marianne's bed, holding her hand and watching her sleep, and she did not stir for hours, though her limbs ached from the long journey. At last Marianne opened her eyes, looked about her in some confusion, smiled weakly and knew her mother at once. The whole room seemed to Elinor to be filled with sunshine, although it was a cold evening and the curtains were drawn.

Day by day Marianne grew stronger, and she began to eat a little, to sit up against her pillows and to talk in a low, calm voice. Mrs Dashwood stayed at Cleveland to nurse her, and in the quiet hours of the afternoon she heard from Elinor the whole story of what had happened in London. She was surprised and moved at every turn, and she often wiped her eyes.

Elinor told her mother of Willoughby's midnight visit and of his sorry tale, and then, because the time had come, she told her about the long secret of Edward and Lucy. Mrs Dashwood, who had hoped for many months that Elinor might marry Edward, was deeply moved by her daughter's courage and angry at the girl who had spoiled her hopes. She took Elinor in her arms and held her tightly for a long time, and for once she could not find a single word.

The Colonel, who had remained at Cleveland to see his friends through their trouble, told Mrs Dashwood in simple words how deeply he loved Marianne, and he asked for nothing in return except permission to hope. Mrs Dashwood, who had grown to value his goodness during the last few days, promised him that she would remember what he had said and that she would never be unkind to him. He thanked her gravely, with a look of quiet gladness that he did not try to hide, and went out to walk in the garden.

Marianne was soon able to sit up in a chair beside the window, and then to walk, with her mother's arm, across the room and back again, which seemed to her a great adventure. Mrs Jennings, who was delighted with the change, gave her every sweet that she could find and a great many that she could not eat. The old woman's face shone with such honest kindness that Marianne, who was too weak for many words, took her hand and kissed it.

One afternoon Marianne asked Elinor to tell her about Willoughby's visit, saying that she wished to hear it all and to hear it from her. Elinor told her gently, leaving out nothing of importance, and Marianne wept quietly as she listened but did not once stop her. When it was over she lay very silent for some time, and then she said, with quiet courage, that she was glad to have heard it.

Marianne saw clearly at last how wrong her own behaviour had been, for she had given way to her feelings without a thought for the pain that she had caused her family. She grieved that she had nearly killed herself with her own sorrow and that she had walked in the wet grass at Cleveland with no thought for her health. She said that she was deeply ashamed of her own conduct, and she begged them all to forgive her and to be patient with her.

At last the doctor allowed them to travel, and they left Cleveland and went home to Devonshire in the Colonel's carriage, which he had insisted upon lending them. He rode beside them for part of the way, in great concern for Marianne's comfort, and when the time came for them to separate he stopped his horse and bade them a kind and quiet farewell. Marianne leaned from the window of the carriage and gave him her hand, and she thanked him in a low and grateful voice.

At Barton Marianne walked slowly round the little garden on her mother's arm, and the sight of the old paths and the windows of the cottage brought back a flood of memories of the happy days with Willoughby. She wept for a few minutes, because there was no help for it, but then she dried her eyes and smiled at the green hills that rose behind the house. It was her first smile of real peace for many months, and her mother, who saw it, pressed her arm.

Back in Barton Cottage Marianne decided, with great seriousness, that she would read, study and live with more calm, and she made a list of the books that she meant to finish by the summer. She thanked Elinor warmly for her care, and she told her that she would never forget how she had sat by her bed day and night. Elinor, who was not at all used to being thanked, laughed and blushed and said that it had been no trouble.

The days at Barton were peaceful, and Marianne's pale cheeks began to glow again as she grew stronger in the mild spring air. She read for hours each morning, took long walks along the lanes in the afternoon and practised her music in the evening with a gentleness that she had never shown before. Mrs Dashwood, who watched her recovery with deep thankfulness, felt her own spirits lift with it.

Mrs Dashwood, however, began to worry about Elinor, who had grown quiet and tired and seemed to take little pleasure in anything. She noticed that her eldest daughter often sat with her work idle in her lap and that her eyes seemed to follow something far away. It was plain that Elinor thought of Edward whenever she believed that no one was watching her.

One morning Thomas, the manservant, returned from an errand to Exeter with some news that he could not wait to share, and he stopped in the kitchen to tell the whole household. He said that he had met Mr Ferrars there, walking with the lady who had been Miss Steele, and that they were now married and on their way to Plymouth. The news ran through the little house like fire through dry grass, and it reached Elinor in the parlour before anyone could stop it.

Elinor was stunned by the news, and although she tried hard to remain calm in front of the others, she could not hold back a sudden pallor. She said that she wished to be alone, walked quietly up the stairs and shut the door of her room, and then she wept for a very long time. It was the first time in many months that she had allowed herself to cry without restraint.

Mrs Dashwood, who now knew everything, went softly up to her daughter's room and sat beside her on the bed, and she comforted her without saying a single word. She wished with all her heart that she had seen the sorrow earlier, for she knew how long the child had carried it alone, and she felt the bitterness of her own blindness. Elinor leaned her head upon her mother's shoulder and, for the first time in many weeks, was truly comforted.

That evening Marianne, who had been thinking a great deal, told Elinor that she was proud of her patience and that she wished she might learn to bear her troubles half so well. She said that she hoped with all her heart that nothing so sad would ever happen to her sister again, and that she would be a better sister to her from now on. Elinor, who had not expected such kind words, smiled through her tears and pressed her sister's hand.

A few days later, as the family sat in the parlour in the soft light of the afternoon, a man on horseback rode up to the garden gate and dismounted slowly. Elinor, who happened to be looking out of the window, saw to her utter astonishment that the rider was Edward Ferrars himself, and she stood quite still. Her heart, which had been quiet for so long, began to beat so hard that she feared the others would hear it.

Edward came in looking shy and anxious, and he hardly seemed to know where to look or what to say, and he bowed awkwardly to Mrs Dashwood. The family received him politely, but with a surprise and an embarrassment that were quite impossible to hide, since they all believed that he was the husband of another woman. Nobody asked him to sit down for some time, and the clock ticked loudly in the silence.

After an awkward silence Edward said, in a low voice that shook slightly, that he was not married to Lucy Steele, and that his brother Robert was her husband instead. He explained that he had come as soon as he was free to do so, because he had so much to say and had not dared to write it. The words fell into the little room like a stone dropped into a still pond.

Elinor, who could not trust herself to speak or even to stay in her seat, ran out of the room in tears of mingled relief and joy, and she did not stop until she reached the garden. The rest of the family were left looking at each other in amazement, and for several moments nobody knew what to say or what to do. Margaret, who was sitting by the window and had understood more than anyone supposed, was the first to laugh aloud.

Edward explained, with an honesty that cost him some embarrassment, that Lucy had chosen his brother Robert as soon as Robert became the rich son and heir of the family. She had always loved money more than any man, and when the chance had come she had not hesitated to take it. He himself was free at last, and he turned to Elinor and asked, in a voice that shook, whether she would marry him.

Elinor accepted with tears of happiness, and Edward told her, in words that came tumbling out as if they had waited a long time, that he had loved her since the first week at Norland. She said that she had hoped it, though she had never dared to believe it, and that she had loved him just as long. They sat together in the garden for an hour, and neither noticed the time.

Mrs Dashwood was overjoyed when she heard the news, and she kissed them both and declared that she had never been so happy since the day she lost her husband. Edward then told her that he would soon be ordained as a clergyman and that he would live at Delaford, where he would work among poor and simple people. It seemed to her that a better fate had never been prepared for a worthy man.

In time Mrs Ferrars forgave Edward, as proud and angry women sometimes do when they have no better course left to them, and she gave him ten thousand pounds, so that he and Elinor might marry in comfort. She did not approve of the match, nor did she pretend to, but she saw that her son was happier than she had ever known him. The reconciliation was never very warm, yet it was real, and it lasted for the rest of her long life.

Edward and Elinor were married in the little church near the cottage, and they settled at the parsonage in Delaford, which they found very comfortable and a good deal larger than they had expected. Their house was always full of friends and relations, their garden grew fine roses, and they were never in want of the little they needed. Elinor said that she had never known so much happiness could come from so little money.

Colonel Brandon came to Barton often during the months that followed, and little by little Marianne began to value his goodness at its true worth. She saw that he was patient, honest and kind, and that he had loved her through every trial without asking for anything in return. She found, to her own surprise, that she looked forward to his visits and was sorry when he left.

At last Marianne saw that the Colonel's steady kindness was worth far more than all of Willoughby's brilliance and charm, which had faded like a bright dream. She understood that she had been wrong to ask for so much sparkle and so little truth, and she said so to Elinor with a candour that made them both laugh. A new and quieter feeling had grown in her heart, and she did not try to resist it.

Willoughby, who had married Miss Grey for her fortune, was unhappy with his rich wife, who was cold and quick to anger, and he found that money did not buy contentment. He regretted losing Marianne all his life, although he never said so to anyone, and he was seen to be silent whenever her name was spoken. It was a lonely end for a man who had once had everything that he wanted.

Marianne, at nineteen, married Colonel Brandon, to her own surprise and to the great delight of her mother, and she became the pride of Delaford and the friend of the whole neighbourhood. She gave him her whole heart, as she did everything, and she found in the quiet devotion of a good man a happiness that she had never thought to find. The wedding took place in the spring, and the bride was by all accounts as lovely as the morning.

Both sisters lived happily near one another at Delaford, with a walk of only a short distance between the Colonel's house and the parsonage, and their families visited each other almost every day. Elinor and Marianne remained the closest of friends all their lives, and they never forgot what they had suffered together, nor how much each had learned from the other. The one had taught the other to feel, and the other had taught her to wait.
